title: Energy at work: how energy makes things happen, and why a still table has energy too

summary.text: Put a wet coin on an empty bottle from the freezer, and the coin starts to click with nobody touching it. A bottle that was not in the freezer does nothing. Why? In this lesson you will test this yourself, look for energy in a still table, and join machines in an energy chain.
summary.art: A clear empty bottle, misted with cold, standing on a wooden table with a coin on its mouth lifted slightly at one edge, and a girl leaning in to watch with her hands behind her back.

intro.hook: A fan needs electricity. A scooter needs petrol. You need breakfast. A table needs nothing and does nothing. So does a table have any energy at all?
intro.text: Energy is what makes things happen. In this lesson you watch a kitchen at work and find where the energy for each thing comes from. You find that a mixie, a stove and your own body all do the same job. They take energy in one form and give it out in another. Then you test the table. You put a cold bottle on it and a coin on the bottle, and you count what happens. By the end you can say what energy a still table has, and why that energy usually does nothing.
intro.art: A kitchen in an Indian flat with a mixie running, a pressure cooker on a gas stove and a ceiling fan turning, and in the middle a plain wooden table with nothing on it.

outcomes: I can say what energy does, and find energy moving, lighting, sounding, heating and cooling things at home and outside.
I can name the energy that goes into a machine and the energy that comes out, for at least six things at home.
I can name six sources of energy, and follow an energy chain back to the Sun.
I can name four kinds of energy that a still table has.
I can explain, from the Clicking Coin Test, that energy makes something happen only when it moves from one thing to another.
I can explain, from the Fan and the Ice, what a fan really does, and why moving air cools me.
I can follow five rules for using electricity safely, and say what would stop in my town without electricity.
I can tell how Sadi Carnot found that heat does work only by passing from a hot place to a cold one.

terms.meaning: What is needed to make anything happen. Energy makes things move, light up, make a sound, get hotter or cooler, and do work.
terms.example: Energy from cooking gas heats the milk. Energy from your breakfast lets you climb the stairs.
terms.art: A pot of milk rising on a gas flame beside a child climbing stairs.

terms.meaning: One of the ways energy shows itself. The main forms are movement, heat, light, sound, electrical energy and stored energy.
terms.example: A television gives out light, sound and a little heat. All three are forms of energy.
terms.art: A television with three small arrows coming out, labelled light, sound and heat.

terms.meaning: Energy going from one form to another. Scientists also call this energy conversion.
terms.example: In a torch, the stored energy of the cell changes to electrical energy, and then to light.
terms.art: A torch cut open to show a cell, a wire and a glowing bulb, joined by arrows.

terms.meaning: Anything that takes energy in one form and gives it out in another. Every machine is an energy changer, and so is every living body.
terms.example: A mixie takes in electrical energy. It gives out movement, sound and heat.
terms.art: A mixie with one arrow going in at the plug and three arrows coming out of the jar.

terms.meaning: Where the energy for something comes from.
terms.example: The Sun, food, fuel, electricity, wind and flowing water are sources of energy we use every day.
terms.art: Six small pictures in a row: the Sun, a plate of idli, a gas cylinder, a wall socket, a pinwheel and a stream.

terms.meaning: A material that gives out heat and light when it burns. A fuel holds stored energy.
terms.example: Cooking gas, petrol, diesel, coal, firewood and the oil in a diya are fuels.
terms.art: A gas cylinder, a petrol pump nozzle, a heap of coal and a lit diya.

terms.meaning: Energy that is kept in something and can come out later.
terms.example: Food, a charged cell, a stretched rubber band and water in a roof tank all hold stored energy.
terms.art: A stretched rubber band, a cell, a banana and a roof tank drawn side by side.

terms.meaning: Energy stored in the way the atoms of a material are joined. It comes out when the material burns or is digested.
terms.example: Rice, petrol, wood and the chemicals in a cell hold chemical energy.
terms.art: A grain of rice and a log of wood, each with a zoom-in circle showing small balls joined by sticks.

terms.meaning: A line of arrows that shows where energy came from, step by step.
terms.example: Sun → paddy plant → rice → your muscles → the pedals of a cycle.
terms.art: Five small pictures joined by arrows: the Sun, a paddy plant, a plate of rice, a leg muscle and a bicycle pedal.

terms.meaning: The energy of the moving particles inside a thing. The faster the particles move, the hotter the thing is. Scientists also call it thermal energy.
terms.example: A table at room temperature holds heat energy. A spoonful of hot tea holds more heat energy than a spoonful-sized piece of the table, because the tea is hotter.
terms.art: A wooden table with a zoom-in circle showing tiny balls shaking in place, with short lines to show movement.

terms.meaning: A very tiny piece of matter, far too small to see. Atoms and molecules are particles.
terms.example: The air in a bottle is made of particles that fly about and hit the walls.
terms.art: An empty bottle with a zoom-in circle showing dots with small arrows flying in all directions.

terms.meaning: The coldest temperature there can be: about 273 degrees below zero on the Celsius scale. At that temperature, particles have the least movement they can ever have.
terms.example: A room at 27 degrees is 300 degrees above absolute zero. So everything in the room holds a lot of heat energy.
terms.art: A tall thermometer with three marks: minus 273 degrees at the bottom, 0 degrees for ice, and 27 degrees for a room near the top.

terms.meaning: A form of energy that travels through wires. It is easy to send far and easy to change into other forms.
terms.example: Electricity runs the fan, the fridge, the lights and the water pump.
terms.art: A wall socket with a wire leading to a fan, a bulb and a fridge.

terms.meaning: A place where electricity is made from another source of energy, such as coal, falling water, wind or sunlight.
terms.example: The Neyveli power station in Tamil Nadu burns a soft brown coal called lignite to make electricity.
terms.art: A power station with tall chimneys and cooling towers, and electricity pylons leading away from it.

terms.meaning: A wheel with blades. Moving steam, water or wind pushes the blades and turns the wheel.
terms.example: In a dam, falling water turns a turbine.
terms.art: A wheel with curved blades inside a pipe, with arrows of water pushing the blades round.

terms.meaning: A machine that changes movement into electrical energy. A turbine turns the generator.
terms.example: A cycle dynamo is a small generator. The turning wheel makes the lamp light up.
terms.art: A bicycle wheel turning a small dynamo with a wire to a glowing lamp.

terms.meaning: A machine at home that runs on electricity or fuel and does one job.
terms.example: A fan, a mixie, an iron, a fridge and a gas stove are appliances.
terms.art: A fan, a mixie, an iron and a fridge in a row.

terms.meaning: How much of the energy going into a machine does the job we want. An efficient machine wastes less.
terms.example: A 9 watt LED bulb gives about the same light as an old 60 watt bulb. So the LED bulb needs far less electrical energy to do the same job.
terms.art: An LED bulb and an old glass bulb glowing equally bright, with a small 9 under one and 60 under the other.

terms.meaning: Electricity made without smoke or harmful gases, from sunlight, wind or flowing water.
terms.example: Solar panels on a roof make clean energy.
terms.art: Solar panels on a flat roof with a wind turbine on a hill behind.

terms.meaning: Harmful smoke, gases or waste that make the air, water or land dirty.
terms.example: Smoke from burning coal and wood pollutes the air.
terms.art: Grey smoke rising from a chimney over a row of houses.

explanations.definition: Energy is what is needed to make anything happen. It makes things move, light up, make a sound, get hotter or cooler, and do work.
explanations.description: You cannot see energy itself. You see what it does. In a kitchen you can find all of it in five minutes. The mixie blades move. The flame gives light and heat. The cooker whistles. The fridge cools the curd. Doing work is one more thing energy does. In science, work means moving something with a push or a pull, such as lifting a bucket or grinding batter. When nothing at all is happening to a thing, no energy is moving in or out of it. That does not mean the thing has no energy, as the table will show.
examples: Moving: a ceiling fan, a scooter, a kite on the wind, a running dog.
Lighting up: a tube light, a diya, a firefly, the Sun.
Making a sound: a cooker whistle, a mridangam, a temple bell, a koel calling.
Heating and cooling: a gas stove, an iron, a fridge, a clay pot of water.
Doing work: a lift carrying people up, a pump filling the roof tank, you carrying a school bag.
explanations.art: A kitchen scene with five labelled arrows pointing at a mixie, a flame, a cooker whistle, a fridge and a hand lifting a pot.

explanations.concept: Every working thing is an energy changer
explanations.definition: An energy changer takes energy in one form and gives it out in another. No machine makes energy, and no machine uses energy up.
explanations.description: Ask two questions about any working thing. What energy goes in? What energy comes out? A fan takes in electrical energy and gives out movement, with a little heat and sound. A gas stove takes in the chemical energy of cooking gas and gives out heat and light. A loudspeaker takes in electrical energy and gives out sound. Your body is a changer too. It takes in the chemical energy of food and gives out movement, heat and sound. Often one form is what we wanted, and the rest is given out as warmth that nobody asked for. Add up everything that comes out, and it equals what went in.
examples: A mixie takes in electrical energy. It gives out movement, sound and heat.
An electric iron takes in electrical energy. It gives out heat.
A scooter engine takes in the chemical energy of petrol. It gives out movement, heat and sound.
A solar panel takes in light. It gives out electrical energy.
A child running takes in the chemical energy of food. She gives out movement and heat.
explanations.art: A row of four machines, each drawn as a box with one labelled arrow going in on the left and two or three labelled arrows coming out on the right.

explanations.concept: Six sources of energy we use every day
explanations.definition: A source of energy is where the energy for something comes from. At home and in town we use the Sun, food, fuel, electricity, wind and flowing water.
explanations.description: The Sun dries clothes and papads, warms water on a roof and lights the day. Food gives energy to every animal, including us. Fuels are burned for heat or movement. Cooking gas runs the stove, petrol runs a scooter, diesel runs a bus, coal feeds a power station, and oil feeds a diya. Electricity runs fans, lights, pumps and phones. Wind dries clothes, lifts kites, moves sailing boats and turns wind turbines. Flowing and falling water turns the turbines in dams. In the hills of Uttarakhand, a stream turns the stone of a small flour mill called a gharat. Electricity is a special case. Nobody finds electricity in nature ready to use. It is always made from one of the other sources, and wires carry it to us.
examples: The Sun dries clothes on a line, heats water in a solar water heater, and dries sea water into salt in the salt pans near Thoothukudi.
Food gives energy to a child who is cycling, to a bullock pulling a cart and to a crow flying.
Fuel gives energy to an LPG stove, to an auto that runs on CNG and to a diesel lorry.
Electricity gives energy to a fan, to a lift and to a metro train.
Wind lifts a kite at Uttarayan, and it turns a wind turbine near Kanyakumari.
Flowing water turns the turbines at the Idukki dam in Kerala, and it turns the stone of a gharat in the hills.
explanations.art: Six panels: clothes drying in sunshine, a girl eating dosa, a gas stove, a fan with a plug, wind turbines on a ridge and water falling through a dam.

explanations.concept: Follow the energy back: an energy chain
explanations.definition: An energy chain is a line of arrows that shows where energy came from, step by step. Most chains on Earth start at the Sun.
explanations.description: Start with something happening and keep asking where its energy came from. A child pedals a cycle. Her muscles got the energy from rice. The paddy plant made the rice using sunlight. So the chain is Sun, paddy plant, rice, muscles, pedals. Try a fan. Its electricity came from a power station. The power station burned coal. Coal is the remains of forests that grew about 300 million years ago, and those trees grew with sunlight. Petrol and cooking gas come from tiny sea beings who lived long ago, and they also lived on sunlight. Wind blows because the Sun warms some places more than others. Rivers flow because the Sun lifted the water as vapour. A few chains do not start at the Sun: the heat inside the Earth, the tides and nuclear power.
examples: Sun → paddy plant → rice → muscles → cycle pedals.
Sun → ancient forest → coal → power station → wires → fan.
Sun → warm and cool air → wind → wind turbine → wires → bulb.
Sun → water vapour → rain → river → dam turbine → wires → train.
explanations.art: A long arrow chain across the page: the Sun, a paddy field, a plate of rice, a girl's leg, a cycle pedal.

explanations.definition: Stored energy is energy kept in something, ready to come out later.
explanations.description: Energy does not have to be used at once. A cell stores chemical energy until you switch on the torch. Food stores it until your body needs it. A stretched rubber band stores energy in the stretch. A blown-up balloon stores it in the stretched rubber and the squeezed air. Water pumped up to a roof tank stores energy by being high up. Petrol, coal and wood are stores that took millions of years, or many years, to fill. A store lets us carry energy about and use it when we choose. That is why a phone has a battery and a scooter has a tank.
examples: A charged phone battery holds stored energy until you use the phone.
A wound-up toy or a stretched rubber band holds stored energy in the winding or the stretch.
A full gas cylinder holds stored energy in the gas, which is a fuel.
A roof tank full of water holds stored energy, because the water is high up.
A banana in your school bag holds stored chemical energy that your body can use later.
explanations.art: A phone battery, a stretched rubber band, a gas cylinder, a roof tank and a banana, each with a small clock beside it to show waiting.

explanations.concept: A still table has energy too
explanations.definition: A table that is doing nothing still holds energy in four ways. It holds heat energy, chemical energy, stored energy of height, and energy in its mass.
explanations.description: First, heat energy. The particles of the wood never stop shaking. A room at 27 degrees is 300 degrees above the coldest temperature there can be, so the table holds a lot of heat energy. Very roughly, the heat energy in a 10 kilogram table is about the same as the electrical energy that an iron uses in one hour. Second, chemical energy. Wood burns. Burning that table would give out about 160 million joules. A unit of electricity is what your electricity meter counts, and 160 million joules is about 44 of those units. A tree stored that energy from sunlight. Third, height. A table on the third floor would fall if the floor were not there, so its position stores energy. Fourth, mass. Albert Einstein showed in 1905 that mass itself is a store of energy. The mass of a 10 kilogram table holds as much energy as about 250 billion units of electricity. That is more than all of India uses in a month. Nobody can get that energy out of a table. It is there all the same.
examples: Heat energy: the table melts an ice cube placed on it, with no flame.
Chemical energy: a wooden matchstick is the same material, and it burns.
Stored energy of height: an eraser pushed off the table edge falls and lands with a tap.
Mass: all matter is stored energy, and the Sun shines because it turns a tiny part of its mass into light and heat.
explanations.art: A plain wooden table with four labelled arrows: one to a zoom-in of shaking particles, one to a small flame on a wood chip, one to the gap between the table top and the floor, and one to the symbol E = mc².

explanations.concept: Why the table's energy does nothing
explanations.definition: Energy makes something happen only when it moves from one thing to another or changes form. Heat energy moves only when one thing is warmer than another.
explanations.description: In the Clicking Coin Test, a room-warm bottle stands on the table and the coin never moves. A bottle from the freezer on the same table makes the coin click many times. The table and the air hold the same heat energy both times. With the warm bottle, everything is at one temperature, so no heat energy moves. With the cold bottle there is a difference. Heat energy moves from the warm air and table into the cold air inside the bottle. The warmed air needs more room, so it lifts the coin and a puff escapes. When the bottle is as warm as the room, the clicking stops. The same rule holds for other energy. Water runs a turbine only if it can fall to a lower place. A cell drives a current only while its two ends differ. So a thing can hold a great deal of energy and do nothing with it.
examples: A cold bottle on a warm table: heat energy moves, and the coin clicks.
A warm bottle on a warm table: nothing moves, and nothing happens.
Water in a lake behind a dam: it turns the turbine only when it falls.
Hot tea in a cool room: heat energy moves out until both are the same.
explanations.art: Two bottles on one table: a misted cold bottle with arrows of warmth going into it and a coin jumping, and a plain bottle with no arrows and a still coin.

explanations.concept: Still air is not still inside
explanations.definition: The particles of air fly about all the time, even in a closed room with no breeze. Their movement is the heat energy of the air.
explanations.description: At room temperature, the particles of air move at about 500 metres every second. That is faster than a passenger aeroplane. They move in every direction and hit each other, so the air as a whole goes nowhere. You feel no wind. The air in a small bedroom holds roughly 9 million joules of heat energy. That is about two and a half units of electricity. Warm the air and the particles fly faster and hit the walls harder. In the cold bottle, that is what lifts the coin. Cool a thing and its particles slow down. They would have the least movement they can ever have at absolute zero, about 273 degrees below zero. Even there, physicists have found that a little movement remains. Nothing is ever perfectly still.
examples: Still air in a closed room has particles that fly about at about 500 metres every second.
Air that is warmed in a bottle has faster particles, and they push the coin up.
A steel spoon, a stone and a table are solid, so their particles shake in place.
Liquid helium stays liquid even close to absolute zero, because its particles keep moving.
explanations.art: A quiet bedroom with a zoom-in circle of air showing dots with arrows in every direction, and a small label '500 metres a second'.

explanations.definition: A fan changes electrical energy into the movement of air. It does not make the air colder.
explanations.description: In the Fan and the Ice, an ice cube in the fan's wind melts faster than one in still air. If a fan made air cold, that ice would last longer. A fan only moves the room's air. Moving air brings the room's heat energy to the ice faster. The same wind cools you, because your skin is warmer than the room. At about 33 degrees, your skin gives heat to the cooler air, and moving air carries it away faster. Sweat also dries faster in a wind, and drying takes heat from your skin. On a very hot day, when the air is hotter than your skin, a fan blows heat into you. A fridge and an air conditioner are different. They use electricity to move heat from inside to outside, which is why the back of a fridge is warm. A clay pot cools water with no electricity at all: water seeps through the clay and dries, and drying takes heat away.
examples: A fan in an empty room cools nothing. It warms the room a little.
A wet hand in the fan's wind feels much colder than a dry one.
The back of a fridge is warm: that is the heat moved out of the food.
A matka keeps water cool because water dries off its damp outside.
explanations.art: A table fan blowing on an ice cube on a plate with a pool of melt water, beside a second ice cube behind a cardboard wall that is still large.

explanations.concept: Electricity: how a town gets its energy
explanations.definition: Electricity is made at power stations from other sources of energy, and wires carry it to homes, shops, trains and hospitals.
explanations.description: Most of India's electricity, about 7 units in every 10, still comes from burning coal. The burning coal boils water. The steam turns a turbine, and the turbine turns a generator. Only about one third of the coal's energy becomes electricity. The rest leaves as warmth. Dams, wind turbines and solar panels make most of the rest. Wires on tall towers join the power stations and towns of the whole country in one network, called the grid. Electricity cannot easily be stored, so it is made at the moment it is used. Now think of a town with no electricity for a day. The water pump stops, so the roof tank runs dry. Lifts and metro trains stop. Phone towers and hospital machines run on batteries and diesel generators for a while. Gas stoves, cycles and the Sun go on working.
examples: Coal → heat → steam → turbine → generator → wires → your fan.
Bengaluru's streets were lit by electricity in 1905. The power came from falling water on the Kaveri, far from the city.
A hospital keeps a diesel generator for the hours when the power fails.
A solar street light makes and stores its own electricity.
explanations.art: A map-like picture: a coal power station, a dam and a field of solar panels, all joined by lines of pylons to a small town with houses, a hospital and a train.

explanations.concept: Five rules for using electricity safely
explanations.definition: Electricity from a wall socket is strong enough to kill. Five rules keep you safe.
explanations.description: Rule one: keep water away from electricity. Never touch a switch, a plug or an appliance with wet hands. Rule two: never push a finger, a pin or anything else into a socket. Rule three: never touch a wire that is broken, worn or bare, and tell a grown-up at once. Rule four: stay far away from a fallen wire, an electricity pole and a transformer, and never fly a kite near power lines. Rule five: switch off before you pull a plug out, and pull the plug, not the wire. Your body is mostly water with salts in it, and it carries electricity. That is why the rules matter. The electricity from a wall socket pushes very strongly, so it can send a dangerous current through you. The small cells in a torch push only very weakly, so they are safe to handle.
examples: Dry your hands before you touch the fan switch.
After a storm, a wire lies on the road. Keep away and call a grown-up.
The cover of a socket is cracked. Do not use it. Tell a grown-up.
A kite is stuck on a power line. Leave it there.
explanations.art: Five small panels, each with a green tick or red cross: dry hands on a switch, a pin near a socket, a frayed wire, a kite near power lines, a hand pulling a plug by its body.

explanations.concept: Using energy well, and keeping the air clean
explanations.definition: An efficient machine does the same job with less energy. Clean energy is made without smoke.
explanations.description: Every changer gives out some warmth that nobody wanted. An old glass bulb turns most of its electricity into heat, so it is too hot to touch. An LED bulb gives the same light with about one sixth of the electricity. Burning coal, wood and petrol puts smoke and harmful gases into the air. Smoke from a wood fire inside a kitchen harms the lungs of the person cooking, who is most often a woman. Sunlight, wind and flowing water make electricity without smoke, and they do not run out. So a family can help in two ways: use less, and choose cleaner. Switch off fans and lights in empty rooms. Put a lid on the pot. Dry clothes in the Sun.
examples: Use a 9 watt LED bulb in place of an old 60 watt bulb. You get the same light for much less electricity.
Put a lid on a pot, so that less cooking gas is needed.
Use a solar water heater on the roof in place of an electric geyser.
Walk or cycle for short trips, instead of using a vehicle that burns fuel.
explanations.art: A kitchen with a lidded pot on a small flame and an LED bulb above, and through the window a clothesline in bright sunshine.

explanations.concept: Living bodies are energy changers that never switch off
explanations.definition: Every living being takes in energy and gives it out again, every moment, even while still or asleep.
explanations.description: A sleeping child looks as still as a table. Inside, the heart beats, the lungs fill, and every cell is at work. A resting grown-up uses the energy of food at about 80 to 100 watts, like a bright old bulb left on. Most of it leaves the body as heat. In parts of Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, families keep their cattle on the ground floor and live upstairs. The warmth of the animals' bodies rises and heats the home. Plants are changers too. A leaf takes in light and stores it as the chemical energy of sugar. Many animals also use energy from outside their bodies. A kite, the bird of prey, soars on rising warm air without flapping. A crocodile lies in the sun to warm up.
examples: A sleeping baby is warm to touch: energy is leaving her body as heat.
Cattle on the ground floor warm a mountain home.
A leaf changes light into the stored energy of sugar.
A kite, the bird of prey, circles upward on warm rising air and saves her own energy.
explanations.art: A stone house in the mountains cut open to show cows on the ground floor and a family upstairs, with wavy lines of warmth rising through the floor.

explanations.concept: Will everything one day reach one temperature?
explanations.definition: If heat moves only from warmer things to cooler things, then after a very long time all differences might vanish. Physicists do not agree that the universe will end this way.
explanations.description: In the Clicking Coin Test, the clicks stopped when the bottle matched the room. Hot tea does the same as it cools. Some physicists expect the whole universe to do this on a vast scale. Stars would burn out and heat would spread. In the end nothing would be warmer than anything else, and nothing could happen. They call this the heat death. It would take far longer than the Sun will shine. Other physicists point out that nobody yet knows what dark energy is, or how the universe will keep growing. So the end is still an open question. Nobody alive will see it either way, but the question comes straight from the coin on the bottle.
examples: The coin stops clicking when the bottle matches the room.
Hot tea cools until it matches the room.
A hot spoon in a cold bowl and the bowl reach one temperature.
Stars give out heat and light into cold space, and they slowly use up their fuel.

perspectives.who: Many physicists, using today's best measurements
perspectives.explanation: The universe keeps growing and stars run out of fuel. Heat spreads until no place is warmer than another. This is called the heat death.
We do not yet know what dark energy is. The universe may change in ways we cannot yet predict, so its end is still open.

explanations.art: A row of tiny stars fading to dark over a long strip of paper, with the last panel showing an even grey sky.

agreed.text: Energy is never made and never destroyed. It only moves from place to place and changes form.
agreed.evidence: In every test since the 1840s, the energy counted before a change has matched the energy counted after it.

agreed.text: No machine makes energy. Every machine changes energy that came from somewhere else.
agreed.evidence: For hundreds of years people tried to build machines that run with nothing put in. Every one of them stopped.

agreed.text: Everything above absolute zero holds heat energy, because its particles are moving.
agreed.evidence: Gases push harder on their containers when warmed, and the amount fits the mathematics of moving particles. Tiny grains in water can be seen under a microscope being knocked about by particles.

agreed.text: Heat energy moves by itself only from a warmer thing to a cooler thing.
agreed.evidence: Nobody has ever seen a cup of tea grow hotter by cooling the room around it. In the Clicking Coin Test, the coin clicks only when the bottle is colder than the room.

agreed.text: Almost all the energy we use on Earth came from the Sun.
agreed.evidence: Food, wood, coal, oil, gas, wind and rivers can all be traced back to sunlight. The heat inside the Earth, the tides and nuclear power are the exceptions.

agreed.text: A living body uses energy all the time, including in sleep.
agreed.evidence: A resting person breathes out carbon dioxide and gives off heat without a break. Both can be measured in a closed room.

challenging.claim: A cold thing has no heat energy.
challenging.for: Cold things feel as if all the warmth has gone out of them. We say 'there is no heat in this room'.
challenging.against: Ice at 0 degrees is still 273 degrees above absolute zero, and its particles are moving. A room-warm table feels neither hot nor cold only because it matches the room. An ice cube on the table melts, and the energy for that comes from the table and the air.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a cold thing has any heat energy left.

challenging.claim: A fan makes the air colder.
challenging.for: You feel much cooler in front of a fan, at once.
challenging.against: A thermometer in the fan's wind reads the same as one in still air. In the Fan and the Ice, the ice in the wind melts faster. The fan moves air, and moving air carries heat away from warm skin and towards cold ice.
challenging.context: This card is about what a fan does to the air in a room.

challenging.claim: Electric scooters and trains run on clean energy.
challenging.for: An electric motor makes no smoke where it runs. City air is cleaner where vehicles are electric.
challenging.against: The electricity has to be made somewhere. In India, about 7 units in every 10 come from burning coal, and the smoke comes out at the power station. Electric vehicles are as clean as the electricity that charges them. They get cleaner as more of it comes from the Sun, wind and water.
challenging.context: This card is about whether electric vehicles are clean, and what that depends on.

challenging.claim: The warm sea is full of heat energy, so ships could run on it for nothing.
challenging.who: Inventors, for more than a hundred years
challenging.for: The sea really does hold a huge amount of heat energy. It seems wasteful not to use it.
challenging.against: Heat energy does work only when it can move into something colder. A ship floating in warm water has nothing colder to send the heat to. Where a warm place lies next to a cold place, the heat can be used. At Kavaratti in Lakshadweep, a plant opened in 2005 uses warm surface water and cold deep water to make drinking water from the sea.
challenging.context: This card is about why we cannot simply take the heat energy out of the sea or the air.

challenging.claim: Only humans use energy from outside their own bodies.
challenging.for: Only humans burn fuel, build dams and make electricity.
challenging.against: Kites, the birds of prey, and vultures climb on rising warm air. Albatrosses cross oceans on the wind. Lizards and crocodiles warm their bodies in sunshine. Termites build mounds that the wind and the Sun keep aired. Humans are one of many animals who borrow energy from the world around them.
challenging.context: This card is about whether humans are the only animals who use sunshine, wind and warmth from outside the body.

challenging.claim: A body at rest uses no energy.
challenging.for: A sleeping person does not move, and seems to be doing nothing.
challenging.against: A sleeping body breathes, pumps blood, keeps warm and repairs itself. A resting grown-up uses about 80 to 100 watts all night. That is why we wake up hungry.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a sleeping or resting body uses energy.

big_questions.q: A table holds a lot of heat energy, and it can do nothing with it. Is energy that can do nothing still worth calling energy?
big_questions.hint: Think of what happened when the cold bottle arrived in the Clicking Coin Test.

big_questions.q: The coin stopped clicking when the bottle was as warm as the room. If the whole universe reached one temperature, could anything ever happen again?
big_questions.hint: Think about what makes heat energy move. Some physicists expect this to happen, a very long time from now.

big_questions.q: A table looks still, and its particles never stop moving. Is 'still' a fact about the table, or about how closely you look?
big_questions.hint: Think of a crowd seen from an aeroplane and from the street.

big_questions.q: Electricity is made in one place and used in another. Who lives beside the power station, and who gets the light?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the smoke goes and where the wires go.

big_questions.q: Before engines, most work was done by the muscles of people and other animals. Whose muscles were they, and what changed for them when machines came?
big_questions.hint: Think of grinding batter by hand, drawing water from a well, and bullocks at a plough.

big_questions.q: You are asleep and perfectly still. Your body is using energy as fast as a bright bulb. What is it doing with all of it?
big_questions.hint: Put a hand on your chest. Think of what never stops.

big_questions.q: A crow, a banyan and you all take energy in and pass it on. Does anyone get to keep any?
big_questions.hint: Think of where your body's warmth goes every minute.

story.title: The Can That Ticked
story.note: The village, the milk society and all the people in this story are made up. Women's milk societies like this one are real, and there are many in Erode district in Tamil Nadu. The ticking lid is imagined. It follows the same science as the coin on the cold bottle in the Clicking Coin Test. A real milk can has a heavy lid that fits tightly, and it would not tick like this.
text: The milk society of Kanjikovil opened at half past five, before the sun was up. It was one long room with a veranda, a weighing scale, and a cold room at the back with a thick grey door.
Thenmozhi was ten. Her mother, Selvi, tested the milk that the women of the village brought in. On holidays Thenmozhi came along to write the numbers in the book.

That April the nights were warm and sticky. Rasathi akka, who ran the society, had started keeping the washed measuring cans inside the cold room overnight. It was the only room with a lock. Each can was steel, as tall as a bucket, with a flat steel lid laid on top while the rim was still wet.

On the first morning of the holidays, Thenmozhi helped to carry the cans out to the veranda. She set the last one down by the scale. It was so cold that her fingers left prints in the mist on its side.
Tik.
She looked round. Nobody was near.
Tik. Tik.
The sound came from the can. The flat lid lifted at one edge, as thin as a fingernail, and dropped. Tik.
'It has started again,' said Valli paati, the watchwoman, from her stool. 'Every morning this month. There is something in those cans. I do not touch them until they go quiet.'
Kathir, who was seven and carried the small pails, backed away to the steps. 'It is a pei,' he whispered. 'A ghost. It lives in the cold room and rides out in the cans.'
Thenmozhi's neck prickled. Then she lifted the lid.
The can was empty. It was clean, cold steel, with three drops of water at the bottom. She put the lid back. For a moment nothing happened. Then: tik.
'A gecko,' said paati. 'A small one, under the rim.'
'There is no gecko,' said Thenmozhi. 'There is nothing in it.'
'Then nothing is knocking,' said Kathir, 'and that is worse.'

She sat down on the floor beside the can and counted. In the first minute the lid ticked twenty-two times. In the next minute, fourteen. Then nine. Then the ticks came so far apart that she lost count. By the time the first women arrived with their milk, the can was silent. She put her palm on it. It was no longer cold.
The next morning she was ready. There were six cans. She carried five out from the cold room. The sixth had been forgotten on the veranda all night, and she put it in the row with the others.
Five cans ticked. The sixth sat as still as a stone.
She swapped the lids. The warm can stayed silent under a cold can's lid. So it was not the lids.

She wiped one cold rim dry with her skirt and put the lid back. That can went quiet, and she felt a tiny breath of air on her wrist where the lid did not quite sit. She wet the rim again. Tik. So the water only closed the gap.
Then she wrapped both arms round one ticking can and held it against her. The lid chattered like teeth. Tik-tik-tik-tik. She let go, and it slowed.
'You are feeding it,' said Kathir from the steps.
'Yes,' said Thenmozhi slowly. 'I think I am.'
She went to find her mother. 'Amma, when air gets warm, does it need more room?'
'It does,' said Selvi, without looking up from her glass tubes. 'That is why a balloon swells in the sun.'
'This can is cold.'
'Then what is warm?'
Thenmozhi looked out at the veranda. The morning was warm. The floor was warm. Her own arms were warm. Everything was warm except the air shut inside those five cans.

She came back to Kathir. 'Listen. The can comes out full of cold air. The morning is warmer than that air. So warmth goes into the can, from the floor and the air and my arms. The air inside swells. It lifts the lid and a puff gets out. The lid drops. Tik. Then it happens again, until the inside is as warm as the outside.'
'And the can that stayed out all night?'
'It is already as warm as the morning. Nothing has anywhere to go.'
Kathir thought about it. 'So the morning is doing it.'
'The morning is doing it. The morning could do it every day. It only needs something cold to do it to.'
He was not sure. So she took an empty glass sample bottle from the shelf in the cold room. She stood it on the veranda floor, wet a one-rupee coin on her tongue, and laid it on the bottle's mouth.
The coin hopped. Tik.
Kathir crept closer. He put one finger on the bottle. He put his whole hand round it. Tik-tik-tik.
'I am feeding it,' he said, and he began to laugh.
Valli paati got up from her stool to see. She held the next cold bottle herself, in both hands, with a coin on top, and he counted aloud until it stopped.

After that, nobody at the society waited for the cans to go quiet. On hot mornings the children raced to carry them out first. Whoever set a can down would stand with one hand on the cold steel and listen to the warm morning going in.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Thenmozhi tests one thing at a time. The warm can never ticks, so the ticking needs cold. Swapping lids changes nothing, so it is not the lids. Hugging the can speeds the ticking, so warmth from outside drives it. She works out that the warm morning holds energy all the time. This energy moves, and makes something happen, only where it meets something colder. The can left out all night is as warm as the morning, so nothing moves and nothing happens.
ask: Why did the cans from the cold room tick, when the can left outside all night did not?
Why did the ticking get faster when Thenmozhi wrapped her arms round the can?
Why did every can go quiet after a few minutes?
Thenmozhi swapped the lids and dried one rim. What did each test tell her?
The morning was just as warm on the days before the cans were kept in the cold room. Why did nothing tick then?
Where else at home does something warm meet something cold? What happens there?

A ten-year-old girl in a cotton skirt setting down a tall steel can misted with cold, her fingerprints showing in the mist.
A flat steel lid on the can lifted a hair's width at one edge, with a tiny puff of air drawn beside it.
An old watchwoman on a stool pointing at the can, and a small boy with a pail backing away to the steps.
