games.title: Energy Dominoes: join the changers in a chain
games.context: This is a card game about energy changers. Each card names a thing, the energy that goes into it and the energy that comes out. You join cards in a line, like dominoes, so that what comes out of one card goes into the next.

printables.title: 28 changer cards: each names a thing, its energy IN and its energy OUT
items: The Sun. START CARD. OUT: light, heat.
Paddy plant. IN: light. OUT: stored energy (rice).
Solar panel. IN: light. OUT: electrical.
Clothes on a line in the sunshine. IN: light. OUT: heat.
A child who has eaten idli. IN: stored energy (food). OUT: movement, heat, sound.
A bullock pulling a cart. IN: stored energy (fodder). OUT: movement, heat.
Gas stove. IN: stored energy (cooking gas). OUT: heat, light.
Diya. IN: stored energy (oil). OUT: light, heat.
Scooter engine. IN: stored energy (petrol). OUT: movement, heat, sound.
Torch cell. IN: stored energy (chemicals). OUT: electrical.
Phone on charge. IN: electrical. OUT: stored energy (battery), heat.
LED bulb. IN: electrical. OUT: light, heat.
Ceiling fan. IN: electrical. OUT: movement, heat.
Mixie. IN: electrical. OUT: movement, sound, heat.
Electric iron. IN: electrical. OUT: heat.
Water pump and roof tank. IN: electrical. OUT: stored energy (water lifted high).
Wind turbine. IN: movement (of air). OUT: electrical.
Dam turbine and generator. IN: movement (of falling water). OUT: electrical.
Hands rubbed together. IN: movement. OUT: heat, sound.
Mridangam. IN: movement (of a hand). OUT: sound.
Rubber band pulled back. IN: movement (your pull). OUT: stored energy (stretch).
Pressure cooker whistle. IN: heat. OUT: movement (of steam), sound.
Coal power station boiler and turbine. IN: heat. OUT: movement (of the turbine).
Your eardrum. IN: sound. OUT: movement.
Burning coal. IN: stored energy (coal). OUT: heat, light.
Open tap under a roof tank. IN: stored energy (water lifted high). OUT: movement.

printables.title: 6 form tokens, to remind players of the forms of energy

rules: Copy each card onto a slip of paper, or print and cut them out. Put the card called The Sun face up in the middle. It starts the chain.
Shuffle the other 27 cards. Deal 5 to each player. Put the rest in a pile, face down.
On your turn, add one card to the end of the chain. Your card's IN must match one of the OUT forms of the last card.
Say the link aloud as you play. For example: 'The Sun gives light, and the solar panel takes light.'
If you cannot play, take one card from the pile. If that card fits, you may play it at once.
Another player may ask you to explain a link. If the link is wrong, take your card back and miss the turn.
The first player with no cards wins. If nobody can play and the pile is empty, the player with the fewest cards wins.
Playing alone: use all 28 cards and build the longest chain you can from The Sun. Twelve cards is good. Sixteen is excellent.

setup.art: Paper cards spread on a floor, each with a name and the words IN and OUT, and the card called The Sun placed face up in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Make the 28 cards. Put The Sun in the middle.

setup.art: A child placing a card that says Solar panel, IN light, OUT electrical, next to The Sun card.
setup.caption: 2. Add a card whose IN matches the last card's OUT. Say the link aloud.

setup.art: A line of six cards across the floor: The Sun, Solar panel, Water pump and roof tank, Open tap, Hands rubbed together, and a child's hand adding a seventh.
setup.caption: 3. Keep the chain growing. The first player to run out of cards wins.

flow.do: 1. Make the 28 cards and the 6 tokens. 2. Lay the tokens where everyone can see them. 3. Put The Sun face up in the middle. 4. Deal 5 cards each.
flow.say: Each card is an energy changer. It tells you what goes in and what comes out. We join them so that energy passes from card to card.
flow.kid: Make the cards. Put The Sun in the middle. Take 5 cards. Read what goes IN and what comes OUT of each.
flow.context: This is the first step of Energy Dominoes. You make the changer cards and deal them out.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to add one card to the end of the chain. 2. The IN of your card must match an OUT of the last card. 3. Say the link aloud. 4. Take a card from the pile if you cannot play.
flow.say: What does the last card give out? Do you hold a card that takes that in? Tell me the link in one sentence.
flow.kid: Look at the last card's OUT. Play a card with the same IN. Say the link aloud. If you cannot play, take a card.

ask.q: Which form of energy was the easiest to pass on? Why?
good: Electrical, because so many machines take it in.
Heat came out of almost every card, but few cards take heat in.

flow.parent: Notice together that heat comes out of nearly every card, and that only two cards take heat in. That is a real fact about energy: most of it ends up as warmth, and warmth is hard to use again.

check.q: In Energy Dominoes, the last card is the wind turbine. Which card can follow it?
check.why: A wind turbine gives out electrical energy, and an LED bulb takes electrical energy in. The mridangam takes in movement and the paddy plant takes in light. If you chose the mridangam, look again at what the turbine gives OUT, not what goes into it.

flow.context: This is the main part of Energy Dominoes. You take turns to join changer cards, so that the energy out of one is the energy into the next.

flow.do: 1. When the game ends, read the whole chain aloud from The Sun. 2. Count how many cards gave out heat. 3. Ask where the energy at the end of the chain has gone.
flow.say: Read the chain from the Sun to the last card. How many of these changers gave out heat?
flow.kid: Read your chain aloud from The Sun. Count the cards that gave out heat.

ask.q: Where does the energy go at the end of a chain?
good: It spreads out into the air as warmth.
It is still there, but it is spread too thin to use.

flow.think: Can you build a chain that ends back at a card it has already passed?
flow.context: This is the last step of Energy Dominoes. You read the finished chain aloud and notice how much of the energy became heat.

games.title: Will It Keep Going? Sort the inventor's claims
games.context: This is a card game about where energy comes from and where it goes. Each card describes a machine or a claim. You decide if it goes on because a source feeds it, stops because its energy runs out, or is impossible.

printables.title: 16 claim cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A wind-up toy car runs across the floor, and then stops. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Stops. The wound spring stored energy from your hand. The car spent it, and most of it became heat from friction.

items.f: A swing is pushed once, then left. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Stops. The push gave the swing energy. Friction at the hooks and with the air turns it into heat, so each swing is lower.

items.f: A ball dropped on a floor bounces lower each time. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Stops. Each bounce turns some of the ball's energy into heat and sound.

items.f: A cup of hot tea is left on a table in a cool room. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Stops. Heat moves from the hot tea to the cooler air until they are at the same temperature. Then it cannot warm anything.

items.f: A cycle rolls down a long slope and on to a flat road. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Stops. The energy stored in the height came out as movement. On the flat road, friction turns it into heat.

items.f: A garden lamp charges in the Sun and glows at night. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Goes on, while the Sun shines each day. Sunlight is the source. The battery stores the energy for the night.

items.f: A dam turbine turns every monsoon as rain fills the lake. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Goes on. The Sun lifts water as vapour, rain falls into the lake and the water falls through the turbine.

items.f: A kite stays up while the wind blows. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Goes on, while the wind blows. The wind is the source. It blows because the Sun warms some places more than others.

items.f: A bullock walks in a circle to turn a stone oil press. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Goes on, while she is fed. Her fodder was grown with sunlight, and her muscles turn it into movement.

items.f: A hand-crank torch glows while you turn the handle. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Goes on, while you keep turning. Your muscles, which run on food, supply the energy.

items.f: A clay pot keeps water cool in summer with no electricity. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Goes on, while water seeps out and dries on the outside. Drying takes heat from the pot, and warm air supplies the energy.

items.f: A water wheel drives a pump, and the pump lifts all the water back up to the wheel, for ever. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Impossible. The pump needs more energy than the wheel gives, because every machine wastes some as heat. The loop runs down.

items.f: A car fan charges the car's battery, and the battery runs the fan for ever. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Impossible. Each change wastes some energy as heat. Nothing is put in from outside, so the loop would slow and stop.

items.f: A lamp has a self-charging battery that never needs a charger. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Impossible. A battery can only give out the energy that was put in. A lamp's light and heat would use it up.

items.f: A phone charger gives out more energy than it takes from the wall. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Impossible. A charger gives out less than it takes in, and its warmth shows where the rest goes. No machine makes energy.

items.f: A ship takes heat from warm sea water and leaves colder water behind. Goes on, Stops or Impossible?
items.b: Impossible. Heat does work only as it passes from a warmer place to a colder one. A ship in the sea has no colder place to send it to.

printables.title: 3 sorting labels to put on the table: Goes on, Stops, Impossible
items: Goes on: a source keeps feeding it
Stops: its energy runs out as spread-out heat
Impossible: it makes energy from nothing

rules: Cut out the 16 cards. Put them in a pile with the question side up. Put the three labels on the table.
Take turns to take the top card and read it aloud.
The player says which label it belongs under, and says where the energy comes from, or where it goes.
Turn the card over and check the back. One point for the right label. One more point for the right reason.
If the player is wrong, the next player may try for one point.
The player with the most points when the cards run out wins.
Playing alone: sort all 16 cards under the labels first, then check the backs. 24 points or more is excellent.

setup.art: Three labels in a row on a table: Goes on, Stops and Impossible, with a pile of face-down cards below them.
setup.caption: 1. Put the three labels on the table and the cards face down.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud that says a ship takes heat from the warm sea, and placing it under the label Impossible.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card aloud, say where it belongs, and say why.

setup.art: Two children turning a card over to check the answer on the back, with a score sheet beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check. Score one point for the label and one for the reason.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards and the three labels. 2. Put the labels on the table. 3. Put the cards in a pile with the question side up. 4. Read the three labels aloud.
flow.say: Every card has a machine or a claim. We sort them into Goes on, Stops and Impossible. Read the three labels together first.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and labels. Put the labels on the table. Read them aloud.
flow.context: This is the first step of Will It Keep Going? You make the cards and put the labels on the table.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read a card aloud. 2. The player chooses a label and says where the energy comes from or goes. 3. Turn the card over to check. 4. Score the points.
flow.say: What is the energy doing in this machine? Where is it coming from? Where is it going? Say it in one sentence.
flow.kid: Read a card. Choose a label. Say where the energy comes from or goes.

ask.q: Which label was hardest, and why?
good: Impossible, because the machine looks clever.
Goes on, because I had to name the source.

check.q: In the game, a lamp has a self-charging battery that never needs a charger. Which label is right?
check.why: A battery gives out only the energy that was put in, and the lamp's light and heat use it up. If you chose Goes on, ask what puts new energy in. If you chose Stops, you are close, but the claim says it never stops, which cannot be true.

flow.context: This is the main part of Will It Keep Going? You sort the cards and give reasons.

flow.do: 1. Look at the Impossible pile. 2. Ask what these cards share. 3. Ask the same about the Goes on pile.
flow.say: What do the Impossible cards share? What do the Goes on cards share? Say each in one sentence.
flow.kid: Look at the Impossible pile. What do these cards share?

ask.q: What do all the Goes on cards have?
good: A source feeding them: the Sun, wind, falling water or food.
Energy keeps coming in from outside.

flow.think: Could you build a machine that never stops? What would it need?
flow.context: This is the last step of Will It Keep Going? You look for what the three piles share.

experiments.title: The Clicking Coin Test: does a cold bottle make a coin click?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put a wet coin on the mouth of a glass bottle that stands on a table. You try a room-warm bottle, a fridge-cold bottle and a freezer-cold bottle, and count the clicks. You will find out whether a colder bottle makes the coin click more.
experiments.question: A bottle at room temperature does nothing on a table. Does a cold bottle make a coin click on the same table? Does a colder bottle make it click more?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the coin click on a room-warm bottle, a fridge-cold bottle and a freezer-cold bottle? Which will click most? Write your guesses, and the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same coin, wet in the same way each time. Use bottles of the same size, and stand each one on the same spot of the same table. Never hold a bottle in your hands during a test. Count the clicks for the same time for every bottle. Change only one thing: how cold the bottle starts.

materials.item: three empty, dry glass bottles of the same size with narrow mouths, such as small cold-drink or sauce bottles
a coin that is wider than the bottle's mouth, such as a 5 rupee or 10 rupee coin
a katori of water to wet the coin, and a cloth to hold the cold bottles
a fridge and a freezer
a phone stopwatch
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Cold glass can slip, so hold it with a cloth. Stand the bottle on a flat table and never on a slope. Never pour hot water on a cold bottle, because the glass can crack. Throw away any bottle with a chipped mouth.

schedule.what: Chill two bottles for 30 minutes, then count the clicks for a room-warm, a fridge-cold and a freezer-cold bottle.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

setup.art: Three empty glass bottles in a row on a wooden table, labelled A, B and C, with a katori of water and a coin beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Label three bottles A, B and C. Bottle A stays on the table.

setup.art: A child's hand opening a fridge door and a freezer door, with one glass bottle on the fridge shelf and one in the freezer.
setup.caption: 2. Put bottle B in the fridge and bottle C in the freezer for 30 minutes.

setup.art: A misted cold glass bottle on a table with a wet coin on its mouth lifted slightly at one edge, and a phone stopwatch beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Wet the coin, lay it on the mouth and count the clicks.

flow.do: 1. Label three bottles A, B and C. 2. Put bottle B in the fridge and bottle C in the freezer. 3. Leave bottle A on the table. 4. Ask for guesses and reasons, and write them down.
flow.say: A coin will sit on the mouth of a bottle on our table. Will it move? Will the answer change for a bottle from the fridge or the freezer? Why?
flow.kid: Label three bottles. Put B in the fridge and C in the freezer. Guess which coin will click. Say why.
flow.parent: Glass bottles are safe in the freezer when they are empty. They need at least 30 minutes there. Overnight is also fine. A plastic bottle will not work, because its thin sides give way.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Clicking Coin Test. You label the bottles, chill two of them and make your guesses.

flow.do: 1. Take bottle A. Stand it on the table. 2. Wet one face of the coin with a drop of water. 3. Lay the coin, wet side down, over the mouth. 4. Count clicks for 2 minutes.
flow.say: This bottle has been in the room all day. Watch the coin for two minutes. Count every click. Tell me what you see.
flow.kid: Stand bottle A on the table. Lay a wet coin on the mouth. Count the clicks for 2 minutes.
flow.wait: Leave bottles B and C for 30 minutes before the next step
flow.parent: Expect no clicks, or only one or two when a breeze or a warm hand is near. This bottle is the fair comparison for the other two.
flow.context: This is the room-warm part of the Clicking Coin Test. Here you watch a coin on bottle A, which has stood in the room all day.

flow.do: 1. Take bottle B from the fridge, holding it with a cloth. 2. Stand it on the same spot of the table. 3. Wet the coin and lay it on the mouth. 4. Count clicks for 2 minutes.
flow.say: This bottle comes from the fridge. Watch the coin and count the clicks. How many came in the first half minute?
flow.kid: Take B from the fridge with a cloth. Stand it on the table. Add a wet coin. Count the clicks.

ask.q: What are the table and the room doing to the cold bottle?
good: Giving it warmth.
The room is warmer than the bottle, so warmth goes in.

flow.parent: A fridge bottle usually clicks a few times and stops. If nothing clicks, check that the coin covers the whole mouth and is wet. Then try once more.
flow.context: This is the fridge-cold part of the Clicking Coin Test. Here you count the clicks for bottle B.

flow.do: 1. Take bottle C from the freezer, holding it with a cloth. 2. Stand it on the same spot and add a wet coin. 3. Count clicks in each half minute for 2 minutes. 4. Keep watching until clicks stop.
flow.say: This bottle comes from the freezer. Count the clicks in each half minute. Write all four numbers. Then keep watching until it goes quiet.
flow.kid: Take C from the freezer. Add a wet coin. Count the clicks in each half minute.

check.q: Bottle C clicked more than bottle B. What is the best reason?
options: Bottle C was colder, so more warmth moved in
Bottle C had a bigger coin
check.why: The same room and the same table were warm for both bottles. Bottle C was colder, so more warmth moved into its air every second. If you chose the coin or the weight, look again at the fair test. Only the starting cold was different.

flow.parent: Most freezer bottles click many times in the first minute, and the clicks slow down. The glass mouth may mist. Do not wipe it, or the coin may stop sealing.
flow.context: This is the freezer-cold part of the Clicking Coin Test. Here you count the clicks for bottle C, and see when they stop.

flow.do: 1. When the clicks stop, touch bottle C with your fingertip. 2. Then touch the table. 3. Compare how they feel. 4. Write the time of the last click.
flow.say: The clicking has stopped. Touch the bottle, and then the table. Do they feel the same? What does that tell you?
flow.kid: Touch the bottle. Then touch the table. How does each one feel?

ask.q: Why did the clicking stop?
good: The bottle became as warm as the room.
Nothing was colder any more, so no more warmth moved in.

flow.context: This step of the Clicking Coin Test is after the last click. Here you feel whether the bottle is still colder than the table.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table of clicks together. 2. Ask your child for three sentences. 3. Ask what bottle A tells us about the room. 4. Then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The room-warm bottle had heat energy but its coin never moved. Why?
good: Nothing was colder, so no heat moved.
Heat energy moves only between a warmer thing and a cooler thing.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Clicking Coin Test. Here you say what the clicks show about heat energy and the table.

experiments.title: The Fan and the Ice: does a fan make the air colder?
experiments.context: In this experiment two ice cubes melt on two steel plates. One cube sits in the wind of a fan, and the other sits behind a screen. You then test a wet hand and a dry hand in the same wind. You will find out whether a fan makes air colder, or only moves it. You will find out whether a fan makes air colder, or only moves it.
experiments.question: Does a fan make the air colder? Does an ice cube last longer in a fan's wind, or melt faster?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the cube in the wind melt faster, slower or at the same speed as the cube behind the screen? Write your guess, and the reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Cut the screen from cardboard and stand it between the fan and one plate. Use two ice cubes from the same tray and two identical plates. Put both plates on the same table. Check the cubes every 2 minutes. Change only one thing: whether the wind reaches the cube.
results_table: Size left of the cube in the wind (0 to 4)
Size left of the cube behind the screen (0 to 4)

materials.item: two ice cubes of the same size, from the same tray (keep them in the freezer until the last minute)
two identical flat steel plates, or two thali plates
a table fan, or a ceiling fan with a table under it
a piece of cardboard or a large open book, about 30 centimetres tall, to make a wind screen
a strip of tissue paper or thread, to show where the wind blows
a phone stopwatch, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Keep water and wet hands away from the fan, its plug and its switch. Dry your hands before you touch the fan switch. Let a grown-up switch the fan on and off.

schedule.what: Melt two ice cubes, one in the wind of a fan and one behind a screen. Then test a wet hand and a dry hand in the wind.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

setup.art: A table with a table fan at one end, a steel plate with an ice cube 60 centimetres in front of it, and a second plate with a cube behind a standing cardboard screen.
setup.caption: 1. Put one plate in the fan's wind and one behind a cardboard screen.

setup.art: A strip of tissue paper hanging still behind the cardboard screen and blowing sideways in front of it.
setup.caption: 2. Check with a paper strip that the wind does not reach the screened plate.

setup.art: A child holding out two hands in front of a fan, one hand with drops of water on its back.
setup.caption: 3. Hold out a dry hand and a wet hand in the wind. Which feels colder?

flow.do: 1. Stand the fan at one end of a table. 2. Stand the screen 60 centimetres from the fan, with the second plate just behind it. 3. Put the first plate in the wind, 60 centimetres from the fan. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: An ice cube will melt in a fan's wind. Another will melt behind a screen. Which will melt faster? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Set up the fan, the screen and two plates. Guess which cube melts faster. Say why.
flow.parent: Hang the tissue strip behind the screen. If it flutters, move the plate closer to the screen or make the screen wider. The fan should be on its fastest setting.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fan and the Ice. You set up the fan, the screen and the plates, and you make a guess.

flow.do: 1. Take both ice cubes from the freezer at the same moment. 2. Put one on each plate. 3. Switch on the fan. 4. Start the stopwatch.
flow.say: Both cubes are the same size and start at the same moment. We start the clock when the fan comes on.
flow.kid: Put a cube on each plate. Switch on the fan. Start the stopwatch.
flow.parent: Let a grown-up switch on the fan, with dry hands. Put both cubes down together.
flow.context: This is the start of the melting in the Fan and the Ice. Here you put the cubes down and start the clock.

flow.do: 1. Look at both cubes every 2 minutes. 2. Give each a size from 4 (whole) to 0 (gone). 3. Write the sizes in the table. 4. Stop when both are gone, or after 20 minutes.
flow.say: Look at both cubes every two minutes. Give each one a size from four, which is whole, to zero, which is gone.
flow.kid: Look every 2 minutes. Give each cube a size from 4 to 0. Write it down.

ask.q: Which cube is smaller now, and by how much?
good: The cube in the wind is smaller.
The one in the wind is a size or two lower.

flow.parent: A cube in the wind often melts much sooner than the other, but the gap changes with the room. If both cubes look the same, check that the screen really stops the wind.
flow.context: This is the watching part of the Fan and the Ice. Here you record how fast each cube melts.

flow.do: 1. Switch the fan off, then on. 2. Put a few drops of water on the back of one hand. 3. Hold both hands in the wind. 4. Say which hand feels colder.
flow.say: Wet the back of one hand. Hold both hands in the wind. Which one feels colder? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Wet the back of one hand. Hold both hands in the wind.

ask.q: Does the wind feel cool on the dry hand too?
good: Yes, a little.
The dry hand feels cooler than in still air, because the wind takes warmth away.

flow.parent: If you have a thermometer, hold it in the wind and then behind the screen. Both read the same number. The wind does not make the air colder.
flow.context: This is the hand test of the Fan and the Ice. Here a wet hand and a dry hand are held in the same wind.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child for three sentences. 3. Ask what the wind did to the heat in the room. 4. Then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. If the fan made colder air, which cube would last longer?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: What does a fan do to the air in a room?
good: It moves the air.
It carries the room's warmth to cooler things faster, such as the ice or my skin.

check.q: In the Fan and the Ice, the cube in the wind melted faster. Why?
options: Moving air brought the room's warmth to the ice faster
The fan made the air hotter
The fan made the air colder
check.why: The fan does not change how warm the air is. It moves air, and moving air brings the room's heat energy to the ice faster. If you chose colder air, the cube would have lasted longer. If you chose hotter air, remember that a thermometer in the wind reads the same as one in still air.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Fan and the Ice. Here you say what a fan really does.

activities.title: Does a Still Table Have Energy? Three small tests
activities.context: In this activity you ask whether a table that stands still has any energy. You guess first. Then you test three ideas with an ice cube, an eraser and a wooden stick. You will find out if a table that does nothing has energy hiding in it. You will find out if a table that does nothing has energy hiding in it.

materials.item: a table
a steel plate and one ice cube
an eraser
a wooden ice-cream stick, or a wooden matchstick
a box of matches and a small bowl of water
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Only a grown-up lights the match and holds the stick. Burn it over the steel plate, with the bowl of water beside it. Never leave a flame alone.
activities.record: Write your first guess and your reason. Then write what each test showed.

setup.art: A plain wooden table in a flat with a steel plate on it, holding an ice cube that has begun to melt into a small puddle.
setup.caption: 1. Put an ice cube on a steel plate on the table. Watch it for 3 minutes.

setup.art: A child's finger pushing an eraser slowly over the edge of a table, with a small gap below it.
setup.caption: 2. Push an eraser off the table edge and listen.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a wooden stick over a steel plate while it burns with a small flame, and a bowl of water beside it.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up burns a wooden stick over the plate.

flow.do: 1. Ask: does a table that stands still have any energy? 2. Your child answers yes, no or not sure. 3. Ask for a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: This table is not moving, not shining and not making a sound. Does it have any energy? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Does a still table have energy? Say yes, no or not sure. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the table tests. You say what you think before you test anything.

flow.do: 1. Put one ice cube on the steel plate, on the table. 2. Watch it for 3 minutes. 3. Ask where the heat came from that melted it.
flow.say: Nobody has lit a flame. Watch the ice. Is it changing?
flow.kid: Put an ice cube on the plate. Watch it for 3 minutes.

ask.q: What is melting the ice, with no flame?
good: Heat from the plate, the table and the air.
The room is warm, so its heat goes into the ice.

flow.context: This is the ice test. Here a cube melts on the table with no flame, so something must be giving it heat.

flow.do: 1. Hold the eraser on the table edge. 2. Push it slowly over the edge. 3. Listen when it lands. 4. Ask what it could do at the edge that it could not do before.
flow.say: The eraser sat still on the table. Now it falls and taps the floor. What was waiting in it at the edge?
flow.kid: Push the eraser slowly over the edge. Listen when it lands.

ask.q: What could the eraser do at the edge that it could not do flat on the table?
good: Fall and make a sound.
Its height stored energy, which came out as movement and sound.

flow.context: This is the eraser test. Here a still eraser falls and makes a sound, so some energy must have been waiting in it.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up lights the wooden stick over the steel plate. 2. Watch it burn for 10 seconds. 3. Ask what the stick gives out. 4. Put it out in the bowl of water.
flow.say: Most tables are made of wood, like this stick. A grown-up will burn it. Watch what it gives out.
flow.kid: Watch the stick burn. Do not touch it.

ask.q: What does the burning wood give out?
good: Light and heat.
The energy stored in the wood comes out as heat and light.

flow.context: This is the wood test. A table is made of wood, and wood burns, so it gives out heat and light.

flow.do: 1. Look at your first guess. 2. Ask: did any test change your mind? 3. Say we will come back to the table at the end of the unit.
flow.say: Look at your first guess. Did any test change your mind? We will come back to the table at the end of the unit.
flow.kid: Look at your first guess. Did a test change your mind? Say why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the table tests. You check your first guess against what you saw.

activities.title: The Changer Table: what goes in and what comes out?
activities.context: In this activity you study eight things that work at home. For each one you write the energy that goes in, the energy you want out, and the energy you did not want out.

materials.item: paper, a ruler and a pencil
eight working things at home, such as a ceiling fan, a mixie, an LED bulb, a phone charger, a gas stove, a TV, a loudspeaker and an iron

activities.safety: Never touch an iron, a geyser, a stove or a hot pan. Feel warmth only with the back of your hand held 5 centimetres away. Never open any appliance.
activities.record: Keep the finished table. Put a star beside every energy that comes out as heat.

setup.art: A hand-drawn table on paper with four columns headed Thing, Energy in, Energy out that I wanted, and Energy out that I did not want.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table with four columns.

setup.art: A child holding the back of one hand 5 centimetres from a glowing LED bulb in a lamp to feel its warmth.
setup.caption: 2. Feel for warmth with the back of your hand, held 5 centimetres away.

flow.do: 1. Make a table with four columns on paper. 2. Head them Thing, Energy in, Energy out wanted, and Energy out not wanted. 3. Write eight things down the first column.
flow.say: We will look at eight things that work in our home. What energy goes into each one? What comes out?
flow.kid: Make the table. Write eight things in the first column.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Changer Table. You draw the table and choose eight things at home.

flow.do: 1. For each thing, write the energy that goes in. 2. Write the energy that comes out and that you wanted. 3. Ask your child to guess what else comes out. 4. Write the guesses lightly in pencil.
flow.say: For each thing, what energy goes in? What do we want it to give out? What else might come out, that we did not want?
flow.kid: For each thing, write what goes in. Write what you want out. Guess what else comes out.
flow.parent: Use these words: electrical, chemical (food or cooking gas), movement, light, sound, heat. A fan takes in electrical energy and gives out movement of air.
flow.context: This is the filling part of the Changer Table. You write in what goes in and what you want to come out.

flow.do: 1. With a grown-up, hold the back of a hand 5 centimetres from each machine that is on. 2. Feel for warmth. 3. Add a star to every machine that gives out heat you did not ask for. 4. Check your guesses.
flow.say: Hold the back of your hand near each machine, but do not touch. Which ones give out warmth that we did not ask for?
flow.kid: Hold the back of your hand near each machine. Do not touch. Feel for warmth.

ask.q: Which machine gave out the most warmth that we did not ask for?
good: The phone charger or the TV.
The mixie motor, after it ran.

flow.parent: Warmth can also be found in the fan motor, the router or the back of the TV. A running mixie motor is warm after a minute.
flow.context: This is the feeling part of the Changer Table. Here you find which machines give out heat as well.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table. 2. Count how many things gave out heat you did not want. 3. Ask whether any machine gave out more energy than went in. 4. Ask why not.
flow.say: How many things gave out heat that we did not ask for? Could any of them give out more energy than went in? Why not?
flow.kid: Count the things that gave out unwanted heat. Could any give out more than went in?

check.q: In the Changer Table, which energy came out of almost every machine?
check.why: Almost every machine gives out some heat that nobody wanted. If you chose light or sound, look at your star marks again. Most machines have no light or sound at all, but nearly all are a little warm.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Changer Table. Here you look for what all eight things share.

activities.title: Light Out for Half an Hour: what stops and what keeps going?
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up switches off the electricity in your home for half an hour in the daytime. You list what stops, what keeps going and what you can do without electricity. You will find out how much of your home needs electricity.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a window with daylight
a gas stove, a steel pan and a little water, or a flask of tea
a wall clock with hands, or a wrist watch with hands

activities.safety: Do this only in the daytime, with a grown-up. Do not do it if anyone at home uses a medical machine that needs electricity. Keep the fridge door shut. The grown-up lights the stove and handles the main switch.
activities.record: Make three lists: what stopped, what kept going, and what you did instead.

setup.art: A child at a table with a sheet of paper headed Stops, Keeps going and Instead, with a window of daylight beside them and a dark ceiling fan above.
setup.caption: 1. Before the power goes off, guess what will stop.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand turning down the main switch lever on a house electricity box on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up switches off the main switch.

setup.art: A child reading a book by a bright window while a grown-up boils water in a pan on a gas stove.
setup.caption: 3. Work by the window and cook on the gas stove.

flow.do: 1. Write the headings Stops, Keeps going and Instead. 2. Ask your child to guess ten things that will stop. 3. Ask which things will keep going, and why.
flow.say: In a minute, we will switch off the electricity. What will stop? What will keep going? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Write three headings. Guess ten things that will stop. Guess what keeps going.
flow.context: This is the first step of Light Out for Half an Hour. Here you guess what a power cut stops.

flow.do: 1. Pick a daytime hour. 2. A grown-up switches off the main switch. 3. Note the time on a clock with hands. 4. Keep the fridge door shut.
flow.say: The grown-up is switching off the main switch. Note the time. We have half an hour without electricity.
flow.kid: A grown-up switches off the main switch. Note the time on the wall clock.
flow.context: This is the switching-off step of Light Out for Half an Hour. A grown-up cuts the electricity, and you start the half hour.

flow.do: 1. Do three jobs without electricity. 2. Read one page by the window. 3. A grown-up boils water on the gas stove. 4. Walk through the home and write down what has stopped.
flow.say: Read a page by the window. Watch the water boil on the stove. Walk around and write down what has stopped.
flow.kid: Read by the window. Watch the water boil. Walk around and write what has stopped.

ask.q: Which things still worked? What energy ran them?
good: The gas stove ran on cooking gas.
Daylight lit the window. That is energy from the Sun.

flow.parent: Check the roof tank pump and the lift if your building has them. They run on electricity, so they may stop. Write that down too.
flow.context: This is the main part of Light Out for Half an Hour. Here you find what stops and what still works.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up switches the main switch back on. 2. Check what comes back by itself and what must be reset. 3. Ask who in the town would need power most.
flow.say: The power is back. Which things came on by themselves, and which must be switched on again?
flow.kid: Power is back. Check which things restarted.

ask.q: Who needs electricity most in a town?
good: Hospitals, because of machines and lights.
Water pumps, trains and phone towers.

flow.parent: Hospitals, water pumps, the metro and phone towers keep batteries or diesel generators for the first hours.
flow.context: This is the last step of Light Out for Half an Hour. You think about who suffers most when a whole town loses electricity.

activities.title: Danger Spotters: a safety walk with five rules
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home with a grown-up, looking at sockets, wires and switches. You spot places that need fixing and say which rule each one breaks. You will find out which places in your home are risky. You will find out which places in your home are risky.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
a grown-up to walk with you

activities.safety: Look but do not touch any socket, plug or wire. Never touch a wire that is broken, bare or wet. Tell the grown-up at once.
activities.record: Keep the list of places you checked, and the rule each one belongs to. Stick the five rules where the family can see them.

setup.art: A child with a clipboard and a grown-up standing in a kitchen, looking at a socket with several plugs in a multi-plug board on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Walk round the home with a grown-up. Look, but do not touch.

setup.art: A hand-written list of five electricity safety rules with a small drawing beside each rule.
setup.caption: 2. Write the five rules and stick them on a wall.

flow.do: 1. Read the five rules aloud. 2. Ask your child to say each rule in their own words. 3. Ask why each rule matters.
flow.say: Here are five rules for using electricity safely. Say each one in your own words. Why does each one matter?
flow.kid: Read the five rules. Say each in your own words. Say why it matters.
flow.parent: The five rules are about water, pins in sockets, broken wires, fallen wires and poles, and pulling a plug by its body.
flow.context: This is the first step of Danger Spotters. You read the five rules before you walk round.

flow.do: 1. Walk to the kitchen, a bedroom, the bathroom and the balcony. 2. Look at each socket, switch and wire. 3. Mark each one 'safe' or 'needs fixing'. 4. Name the rule it belongs to.
flow.say: In each room, look at the sockets, the switches and the wires. Is each one safe, or does it need fixing? Which rule does it belong to?
flow.kid: Look at the sockets and wires in four rooms. Mark each safe or needs fixing.
flow.parent: Look for a switch near a tap, a board with too many plugs, a wire under a mat, or a cracked cover. A grown-up fixes any problem.
flow.context: This is the walking part of Danger Spotters. Here you check four places at home and name the rule for each.

flow.do: 1. Count how many places need fixing. 2. Ask the grown-up to fix them, or to say how. 3. Choose the one that is most dangerous and say why.
flow.say: How many places need fixing? Which one is the most dangerous? Why?
flow.kid: Count the places that need fixing. Pick the most dangerous. Say why.

ask.q: Why is water so dangerous near electricity?
good: Water with salts in it carries electricity, and so does my body.
Wet hands let electricity pass into the body more easily.

check.q: You see a wire lying on the road after a storm. What should you do?
options: Stay far away and tell a grown-up
check.why: A fallen wire may still carry electricity, and wet ground or a stick can carry it to you. The only safe action is to keep far away and tell a grown-up. If you chose the stick, remember that wet wood carries electricity too.

flow.context: This is the sorting part of Danger Spotters. Here you decide which problem is most dangerous.

activities.title: Before the Machine: ask an older person who did the work
activities.context: In this activity you interview a grandparent, an older neighbour or a teacher. You will find out who did the work before machines. You will find out who did the work before machines. You find out how grinding, washing, carrying water and travelling were done before many machines, and what energy did each job.

materials.item: an older person who is willing to talk
paper and a pencil
a phone voice recorder, if the person agrees

activities.record: Keep the table of jobs, and write one sentence about who did most of the work.

setup.art: A child sitting beside a grandmother on a mat, with a notebook, while she shows how she used to turn a stone hand mill.
setup.caption: 1. Ask an older person how a job was done in the past.

setup.art: A table on paper with three columns headed Job, Before, and Now, with a small picture in each box.
setup.caption: 2. Fill in a table: the job, how it was done before, and how it is done now.

flow.do: 1. Choose three jobs: grinding grain, washing clothes and drawing water. 2. Ask your child to guess what gave the energy before machines. 3. Write the guesses.
flow.say: Before machines, who ground the batter and carried the water? What gave the energy? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Choose three jobs. Guess what gave the energy for each before machines.
flow.context: This is the first step of Before the Machine. You choose three jobs and make a guess.

flow.do: 1. Ask the older person about each job. 2. Ask: who did it, how long it took, and what gave the energy. 3. Write what they say. 4. Ask them what they liked and did not like.
flow.say: How did you grind grain, wash clothes and fetch water when you were young? Who did it? How long did it take?
flow.kid: Ask three questions: who did the job, how long it took, and what gave the energy.
flow.parent: Let them tell stories. Good questions: Who woke up first? Who did the heavy work? What did you eat to get the energy? Do not hurry them.
flow.context: This is the interview part of Before the Machine. Here you ask an older person how each job was done and who did it.

flow.do: 1. Fill in a table with the job, how it was done before, and how it is done now. 2. Write the energy used in each column. 3. Ask who did most of the work before.
flow.say: Now fill in the table. For each job, what energy was used before, and what energy is used now? Who did most of the work?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Write the energy used before, and the energy used now.

ask.q: Where did the energy for the old jobs come from?
good: From people's muscles, which got it from food.
From food, and so from the Sun.

flow.context: This is the table step of Before the Machine. Here you compare how each job was done before and now.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to look at who is named in the table. 2. Ask what changed for them when machines came. 3. Thank the person.
flow.say: Who did most of the work before machines? What changed for them when machines came? Say thank you to the person you asked.
flow.kid: Look at your table. Who did most of the work before? What changed? Say thank you.
flow.context: This is the last step of Before the Machine. You think about who did the work, and what changed for them.

projects.title: The Street Energy Survey: what powers our street?
projects.context: In this three-day project you walk along your street or around your building with a grown-up. You list the energy that is used there, ask three neighbours how they cook, heat water and light their homes, and make one chart. You will find out which energy your street uses most. You will find out which energy your street uses most.

materials.item: paper, a pencil and a clipboard or a book to write on
a grown-up to walk with you
coloured pencils, for the chart

projects.safety: Walk with a grown-up. Stay on the pavement. Never touch a wire, a transformer or a gas cylinder. Ask your neighbours only with a grown-up beside you.

schedule.what: Walk along your street or around your building. Write down every use of energy you can see: lights, fans, vehicles, cooking, water heaters, panels.
Ask three neighbours: what do you cook on, what heats your bath water, and what do you do in a power cut? Write their answers.
Draw a bar chart of the fuels and sources your neighbours use. Write one change that would help the street, and say why.

projects.record: Keep the list from day 1, the answers from day 2 and the bar chart. Write one sentence for each: what is used most, and what you would change.

setup.art: A child with a notebook and a grown-up on a city pavement looking at a solar water heater on a roof, a street light and a gas cylinder on a delivery cycle.
setup.caption: 1. Walk your street and list every use of energy.

setup.art: A child sitting on a doorstep with a notebook, asking a neighbour questions while the neighbour stirs a pot on a gas stove.
setup.caption: 2. Ask three neighbours how they cook and heat water.

setup.art: A hand-drawn bar chart on paper showing four fuels with bars of different heights: cooking gas, electricity, firewood and sunlight.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a bar chart of what the neighbours use.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess which energy is used most on the street, and why. 2. Walk along the street with a grown-up. 3. Write every use of energy you see. 4. Mark where each one comes from.
flow.say: Which kind of energy do you think our street uses most? Why? Let's walk and write down every use of energy we see.
flow.kid: Guess which energy our street uses most. Walk and write down every use you see.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Street Energy Survey. Here you walk and list every use of energy on your street.

flow.do: 1. Ask three neighbours the three questions. 2. Write each answer in a table. 3. Ask each one whether they would change anything, and why.
flow.say: What do you cook on? What heats your bath water? What do you do in a power cut? We would like to learn from you.
flow.kid: Ask three neighbours three questions. Write their answers in a table.
flow.parent: Stay beside your child. Some neighbours may use firewood or kerosene. Do not judge. Note it down and ask why.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Street Energy Survey. Here you ask three neighbours what they use at home.

flow.do: 1. Count how many neighbours use each fuel or source. 2. Make a bar for each one: draw it, or stack pebbles. 3. Ask: which source is used most, and which is cleanest? 4. Write one change you would make.
flow.say: Count how many neighbours use each fuel. Make a bar for each. Which is used most? Which is cleanest?
flow.kid: Make a bar for each fuel. Which is used most?

ask.q: What one change would help the street most, and why?
good: Solar water heaters on roofs, because they use sunlight and no smoke.
Switching off lights in empty rooms, which saves electricity.

flow.context: This is day 3 of the Street Energy Survey. Here you make a chart and say what you would change.

challenges.title: Most Clicks: make the coin click as many times as you can
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In the Clicking Coin Test, a coin clicked on a freezer bottle for a few minutes. Here you change one thing at a time to make the coin click more.
challenges.problem: Make a coin click as many times as possible in 3 minutes on a glass bottle. You may change how cold the bottle is, how it is warmed and how the coin is wet.
constraints: Use one coin and one bottle size.
Count the clicks for exactly 3 minutes.
Never pour hot water on a cold bottle.
materials: the glass bottles, coin and cloth from the Clicking Coin Test
a bowl of tap water at room temperature
general: Leave the bottle in the freezer for an hour, not half an hour.
Wet the coin with a thin film of water so that it seals the mouth.
Use a bottle with a narrower mouth.
creative: Stand the cold bottle in a shallow bowl of room-temperature water. Warmth then moves in from all sides, so more clicks come early.
Wrap a cloth wet with lukewarm tap water round the bottle. Never use hot water on cold glass.
Add a second coin on top of the first, and see if the clicks get louder or slower.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way to get the most clicks. Draw your plan, or tell it to your grown-up. Test it twice and write the clicks each time. Which change helped most, and why?

setup.art: A glass bottle from the freezer standing in a shallow bowl of tap water, with a wet coin on its mouth.
setup.caption: 1. Stand a freezer bottle in a shallow bowl of room-temperature water.

setup.art: A child tallying clicks on paper next to a phone stopwatch showing 3 minutes, while a coin lifts on a bottle.
setup.caption: 2. Count the clicks for exactly 3 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Chill the bottle for 30 minutes. 2. Count clicks for 3 minutes on the table, with a wet coin. 3. Write the number. This is the number to beat.
flow.say: First we need the number to beat. How many clicks come in three minutes on the table? Write it down.
flow.kid: Chill the bottle. Count clicks for 3 minutes. Write the number to beat.
flow.context: This is the first step of Most Clicks. Here you count the clicks with no changes, to find the number to beat.

flow.do: 1. Look at the usual ideas: a longer chill, a thin film of water, a wetter coin. 2. Your child chooses one and says why it should work. 3. Test it and write the clicks.
flow.say: Which idea do you think will give more clicks? Why? Test it, and write the number.
flow.kid: Choose one idea. Say why it should work. Test it. Write the clicks.

ask.q: Which one change gave the most clicks?
good: A longer chill.
A bowl of water, because warmth moves in faster.

flow.context: This is the testing part of Most Clicks. Here you try one usual idea and count the clicks.

flow.do: 1. Try one creative idea, such as the bowl of room-temperature water. 2. Test twice. 3. Compare the clicks with the number to beat. 4. Write what you found.
flow.say: Now try your own idea. Why might it work? Test it twice and compare with the number to beat.
flow.kid: Try one creative idea. Test it twice. Compare with the number to beat.
flow.parent: Warmer surroundings make heat move in faster. So the clicks come faster, but they also stop sooner. The total in 3 minutes may be the same. This is a good thing to notice.
flow.context: This is the design part of Most Clicks. Here you test your own idea and compare it with the first count.

challenges.title: The Sail Race: cross a tray with wind alone
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In the Fan and the Ice, a fan moved air that carried heat. Here the moving air does a different job. It pushes a small boat across a tray of water.
challenges.problem: Make a boat that crosses a tray of water, 50 centimetres, in the fewest seconds. Only the wind of a table fan may push it, from a fixed spot.
constraints: The boat is at most 10 centimetres tall.
The fan stays at the same distance and the same setting every time.
Nobody touches the boat after it starts.
materials: a large steel tray or tub, filled with 2 centimetres of water
a table fan on a dry stool
a sheet of aluminium foil, a thin piece of thermocol or a matchbox
thin card or stiff paper for sails
a straw, sticky tape and clay
a ruler and a phone stopwatch
general: A foil boat with one square card sail.
A boat from a matchbox with a straw mast.
Fold the sail so that it faces the wind.
creative: Use two small sails instead of one big one, and compare.
Curve the sail like a cup, to catch more wind.
Add a little clay under the boat for balance, so it does not tip.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own wind boat. Draw it or describe it to your grown-up, build it and race it 3 times. What was the average time? Why did the best sail work?

setup.art: A steel tray of water on a towel-covered table, with a small foil boat with a card sail at one end and a table fan on a dry stool 1 metre away.
setup.caption: 1. Fill a tray and set up the fan 1 metre from the boat.

setup.art: Three different boats on the table: one with a small sail, one with a big sail and one with a curved sail.
setup.caption: 2. Build boats with different sails.

flow.do: 1. Put the towel on the table and the tray on it. 2. Fill the tray with 2 centimetres of water. 3. Stand the fan on a dry stool 1 metre from the start. 4. Mark the finish 50 centimetres away.
flow.say: Water and electricity must stay apart. The fan stands on a dry stool, one metre away. Where is the finish line?
flow.kid: Put the tray on a towel. Stand the fan on a dry stool. Mark a 50 cm finish.
flow.parent: Keep the fan cable well away from the water. Dry your hands before you touch the fan switch.
flow.context: This is the set-up step of the Sail Race. Here you place the tray, the fan and the finish line with a grown-up.

flow.do: 1. Build a foil boat with one card sail, 8 centimetres square. 2. Place it at the start. 3. Switch on the fan. 4. Time the crossing, 3 times.
flow.say: Build the first boat. How long will it take to cross? Why? Time it three times.
flow.kid: Build a boat with one card sail. Time 3 crossings.
flow.context: This is the first race of the Sail Race. Here you time one boat with one sail three times.

flow.do: 1. Change one thing: the size of the sail, its shape or the weight. 2. Time 3 crossings. 3. Add the 3 times and divide by 3 to get the average. 4. Say where the boat's movement energy came from.
flow.say: Change one thing about the boat. Time three crossings.
flow.kid: Change one thing. Time 3 crossings.

ask.q: Where did the boat's movement energy come from?
good: From the fan's electrical energy, through moving air.
The fan changed electrical energy into moving air, and the sail caught it.

flow.context: This is the improving part of the Sail Race. Here you test one change and trace where the boat's energy came from.

worksheets.title: Energy at work: changers, sources and the table (core)

items.p: Which sentence about energy is true?
items.why: Energy is what is needed to make anything happen. It makes things move, light up, make a sound, get hotter or cooler. It is not a liquid and it is not used up. A bulb changes electrical energy into light and heat.
opts: Energy is a liquid in wires
Energy is only in moving things
Energy is used up by a bulb

items.p: True or false: a machine makes new energy.
items.why: False. A machine only changes energy from one form to another. A fan takes in electrical energy and gives out movement and a little heat.

items.p: Match each thing to the energy that goes into it.
items.why: Each machine takes in one form of energy. The fan takes electrical energy. The stove takes the chemical energy of its gas. A solar panel takes light. The wind turbine takes movement of air. Leg muscles take the chemical energy of food.

items.p: Sort these sources of energy by how quickly they are renewed.
items.why: Sunlight, wind and flowing river water are renewed every day by the Sun. Coal, petrol and cooking gas took millions of years to form, so we use them far faster than they come back.
cats: Took millions of years to form
items: Took millions of years to form
Took millions of years to form
Took millions of years to form

items.p: Put these in order, starting from the Sun.
a: The pedals of a cycle turn
items.why: Most chains start at the Sun. Sunlight lets the paddy grow, the rice feeds the rider, and the rider's muscles turn the pedals.
items: The pedals of a cycle turn

items.p: A still table has heat energy, because its ____ never stop shaking.
items.why: The tiny particles that the wood is made of keep shaking all the time. That shaking is heat energy. 'Atoms' and 'molecules' are also right.

items.p: Which of these does an ordinary wooden table NOT have?
items.why: A table has heat energy, chemical energy in the wood, stored energy of its height and energy in its mass. No electricity flows through it unless it is wired up.

items.p: True or false: if a thing holds a lot of energy, it must be doing something.
items.why: False. A still table holds a great deal of energy and does nothing. Energy makes something happen only when it moves or changes form.

items.p: In the Clicking Coin Test, why did the coin on the room-warm bottle never click?
items.why: The bottle held plenty of heat energy, but nothing around it was colder, so no heat moved in. If you chose 'no heat energy', remember that a room-warm bottle is far above absolute zero.
opts: Bottle and room were the same temperature
The room-warm bottle had no heat energy

items.p: Three of these show energy changing form. Which one shows no change?
items.why: A mixie turns electrical energy into movement. A solar panel turns light into electricity. A diya turns the energy of oil into light and heat. A shut cupboard just stands there.

items.p: Name the energy that goes into a ceiling fan and the energy that comes out. Which part did nobody want?
items.a: Electrical energy goes in. Movement of air comes out, with a little sound and heat. The heat in the motor is the part nobody wanted.
items.why: A strong answer names one form going in, and at least two coming out. It names heat as the unwanted part, because the motor feels warm.

items.p: Draw an energy chain from the Sun to a tube light at home. Label each step.
items.a: Any true chain, such as: Sun, solar panel, wires, tube light. Or: Sun, old forest, coal, power station, wires, tube light.
items.why: A strong drawing has arrows in order and a label for each step. It starts at the Sun, and it shows where electricity was made.
items.art: A blank sheet with a small Sun at one end and a tube light at the other, and space for arrows between them.

items.p: On a drawing of a running mixie, label the energy that goes in and three energies that come out.
items.why: A mixie takes in electrical energy. It gives out movement, which is its job, and sound and heat, which are not the job.
items.art: A mixie with its jar, lid and plug, and four blank label lines.

items.p: Write two rules for using electricity safely. Say why each rule matters.
items.a: For example: dry your hands before touching a switch, because wet skin lets electricity pass into the body. Never push a pin into a socket, because the socket carries enough electricity to kill.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different rules and a reason for each. The reason mentions water, the body or the strength of the supply.

items.p: True or false: it is safe to pull a plug out of a socket by tugging its wire.
items.why: False. Tugging the wire can loosen it from the plug and leave bare wire. Switch off first, then hold the plug by its body.

worksheets.title: Why things happen: differences, fans and the grid (stretch)

items.p: A freezer bottle made more clicks than a fridge bottle. Why?
items.why: Both bottles stood in the same warm room. The colder bottle had a bigger gap to the room's temperature, so heat moved in faster and the air expanded faster.
opts: A bigger difference moves heat in faster
The freezer bottle had more air
The freezer made the coin lighter

items.p: A freezer bottle clicked 14, 8 and 4 times in three half-minutes. How many clicks in all?
items.why: 14 + 8 + 4 = 26. The clicks get fewer in each half minute, because the bottle is warming and the gap to the room is closing.

items.p: The clicking stopped after about 4 minutes. Where did the heat go, and why did the clicks stop?
items.a: The heat went from the room into the air in the bottle. Once the bottle was as warm as the room, no more heat moved, so the air stopped swelling and the coin stopped clicking.
items.why: A strong answer says the bottle warmed to the room's temperature, and that heat moves only while one thing is warmer than another.

items.p: True or false: a fan makes the air in a room colder.
items.why: False. A fan only moves air. In the Fan and the Ice, the ice melted faster in the wind, because the wind carried the room's heat to it.

items.p: In the Fan and the Ice, which is the best reason for the faster melting?
items.why: The fan did not make the air colder, or the cube would have lasted longer. It moved the room's air, so more warmth reached the ice every minute.
opts: Moving air brought the room's heat to the ice faster
The fan's motor heated the ice

items.p: Three people talk about the electricity in a country that still burns much coal.
items.a: A strong answer names a fair point for each view. Coal gives steady power and jobs. Smoke harms the lungs of people who live near. Solar is clean, but it needs storage for the night. It picks one view and gives a fair point from another.
items.why: Each view is right about something. A good choice is not to pick a winner, but to say what each side gives up.

views.who: A worker at a coal power station
views.says: Coal gives steady power all night, and my family lives on this job.

views.who: A person who lives near the chimneys
views.says: The smoke makes my children cough. I want cleaner power.
Sunlight is free and clean. But panels only work by day, so we need batteries.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Give one fact as evidence. Then say what one of the others gets right.

items.p: Match each appliance to the energy it is made to give out.
items.why: An iron is made to give heat, a loudspeaker to give sound, a mixie to give movement, an LED bulb to give light. A phone charger gives stored energy to a battery.

items.p: Put these in order to show how the energy of coal reaches a fan.
a: Wires carry electricity to the fan
items.why: The burning coal heats water to steam. The steam turns a turbine, which turns a generator. The electricity then travels through wires to the fan.
items: Wires carry electricity to the fan

items.p: Sort these into energy that can be traced back to the Sun and energy that cannot.
items.why: Coal, food and wind all trace back to sunlight. The heat inside the Earth comes from the Earth itself, and the tides come mostly from the Moon's pull.

items.p: Why does a table on the third floor have more stored energy than the same table on the ground?
items.why: Stored energy of height depends on how far a thing could fall. The same table on the third floor could fall much further, so more energy is stored in its position.

items.p: True or false: a cold thing has no heat energy.
items.why: False. Ice at 0 degrees is about 273 degrees above the coldest temperature there can be, and its particles still move. It has heat energy, only less than warmer things.

items.p: Heat energy can do work only when it passes from a hotter place to a ____ place.
items.why: A hotter place sends heat into a colder one. With no colder place to go, the heat cannot do work, however much of it there is.

items.p: Draw a bicycle dynamo lamp. Add arrows for the energy that goes in and the energy that comes out.
items.a: A wheel turning a dynamo, with a wire to a lamp. An arrow for movement goes in. Arrows for light and heat come out.
items.why: A strong drawing has movement going in, and light and heat coming out. A wheel touching a small dynamo is shown clearly.
items.art: A bicycle wheel with a small dynamo touching its tyre and a wire to a lamp on the front of the cycle, with blank arrows.

items.p: Three of these start with the Sun. Which one does not?
items.why: A wind turbine, a meal of rice and coal all trace back to sunlight. A hot spring is warmed by heat from deep inside the Earth.

items.p: Tea at 80 degrees can warm a cold hand. Tea at 28 degrees in a room at 28 degrees cannot. Why?
items.a: Heat moves only from a warmer thing to a cooler thing. The hot tea is warmer than the hand, so heat moves into the hand. The room-warm tea is the same as the room and the hand, so no heat moves.
items.why: A strong answer says heat moves only when there is a difference in temperature. It names which way the heat moves in each case.

worksheets.title: Reasoning about energy: where it goes and what it can do (challenge)

items.p: A ship takes heat from warm sea water and leaves colder water behind. Why can it not keep going?
items.a: Heat does work only as it passes from a warmer place to a colder place. The ship has no colder place to send the heat to, so it cannot make anything move.
items.why: A strong answer says that heat does work only when it moves from hot to cold. It says the sea around the ship is all at one temperature, like the bottle in the room.

items.p: In 10 hours, a 60 watt bulb uses how many more watt-hours than a 9 watt LED?
items.why: The old bulb uses 60 × 10 = 600 watt-hours. The LED uses 9 × 10 = 90. The difference is 600 − 90 = 510 watt-hours.

items.p: Three people talk about electric scooters.
items.a: A strong answer names a fair point for each. The scooter makes no smoke on the road. The electricity may come from burning coal, so smoke moves to the power station. Cleaner power makes scooters cleaner. It chooses one view and gives a fair point from another.
items.why: All three are right about part of it. An electric vehicle is as clean as the electricity that charges it.

views.says: Electric scooters make no smoke. They are clean.

views.who: A person living near a coal power station
views.says: The smoke has only moved to my town.
Scooters get cleaner as more power comes from the Sun, wind and water.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give one fact. Then say what one of the others gets right.

items.p: A cup of tea cools to room temperature. Where has its heat energy gone?
items.why: Energy is never destroyed. The tea's heat moved into the cooler air and table, which are now a little warmer. It is still there, spread too thin to use.
opts: Into the air and the table

items.p: True or false: the total energy of a closed room stays the same while a hot cup of tea cools in it.
items.why: True. The tea loses heat energy and the air and table gain exactly as much. The total is the same.

items.p: A table never does anything, so it has no energy. Give two pieces of evidence that this is wrong.
items.a: The wood can burn, so it has chemical energy. An ice cube melts on it, so it has heat energy. A table pushed off a high balcony would fall and hit the ground, so its height stores energy.
items.why: A strong answer gives two kinds of energy and an example for each. The ice cube, the burning stick and the falling eraser all work.

items.p: Why does a fan feel cooler when your skin is wet with sweat?
items.why: Drying takes heat from the skin. Moving air carries the wet air away, so sweat dries faster and your skin cools faster. A fan does not make the air colder.
opts: Moving air dries the sweat faster, taking heat
The sweat is colder than the air

items.p: Sort these into energy that is moving and energy that is waiting.
items.why: A whistling cooker, sunlight crossing a room and a cycle going downhill are energy on the move. Coal in a heap, a charged battery and water in a roof tank hold energy that waits.

items.p: Draw two bottles on a table, one cold and one room-warm. Add arrows to show where heat energy moves.
items.a: A cold bottle with an arrow going into it from the table and the air. A room-warm bottle with no arrows.
items.why: A strong drawing shows heat moving into the cold bottle only. The room-warm bottle has no arrows, because the same amount moves in and out.
items.art: Two glass bottles on a wooden table, one misted with cold and one plain, with no arrows drawn yet.

items.p: Put the steps of one click of the coin in order.
a: Heat moves from the room into the cold air in the bottle
The air in the bottle warms and needs more room
The swelling air lifts the coin
A puff escapes and the coin drops
items.why: The warm room gives heat to the cold air. The warmed air swells, lifts the coin and escapes. Then the coin drops, and the click is heard.
items: A puff escapes and the coin drops
The swelling air lifts the coin
Heat moves from the room into the cold air in the bottle
The air in the bottle warms and needs more room

items.p: Match each danger to the right action.
items.why: Each danger has a rule. Fallen wires and kites on power lines are never touched. Wet hands never touch switches. Nothing goes into a socket.
pairs: A wire lies on the road after a storm
Stay far away and tell a grown-up
Dry them before touching a switch
A pin is near a socket
Do not use it, tell a grown-up
A kite is stuck on a power line

items.p: A town has no electricity for a whole day. Which of these still works?
items.why: A gas stove runs on the chemical energy of cooking gas, not on electricity. The pump, the lift and the fridge motor all need electricity.
opts: A gas stove lit with a match

items.p: Almost every energy chain ends as heat in the air. Why is that energy so hard to use again?
items.a: The heat spreads out into a huge amount of air, and the air is only a little warmer. Heat can do work only where there is a difference in temperature, and a little warmth everywhere gives no difference.
items.why: A strong answer says the heat is spread out thinly and has no colder place to flow to. It uses the idea of a difference in temperature.

items.p: True or false: moving air is the same as colder air.
items.why: False. Moving air feels cooler on warm skin because it carries heat away faster. A thermometer in the wind reads the same as one in still air.

items.p: Coal and petrol hold energy that came from ____ long ago.
items.why: Coal is the remains of forests, and petrol comes from tiny sea beings. They lived on sunlight, and their energy was stored for millions of years.

quiz.p: A ceiling fan, a mixie and a loudspeaker all do what with energy?
quiz.why: Every machine is an energy changer. It takes energy in one form and gives it out in others. If you chose 'make new energy', remember that no machine has ever made any.
opts: Change it from one form to another

quiz.p: A phone charger feels warm. Where did the warmth come from?
quiz.why: Every machine gives out a little heat. A warm charger is normal. It shows some of the energy going in has become heat instead of charge.
opts: Some of the electrical energy changed to heat
The charger made heat from nothing

quiz.p: Which chain of energy is in the right order?
quiz.why: Sunlight is the start of most chains. A plant uses sunlight to make rice, and your muscles run on the rice. The other orders put a step before the one that makes it.

quiz.p: Which source of energy does not come from the Sun, even through a long chain?
quiz.why: Wind, coal and rice all trace back to sunlight. Heat from inside the Earth comes from the Earth itself, so a hot spring is not Sun energy.
opts: Heat from deep inside the Earth

quiz.p: A table stands still in a room. Which statement is true?
quiz.why: The particles of the wood always shake, and that is heat energy. A table is still on the outside and busy on the inside.
opts: It holds heat energy, because its particles move
It has no energy until it is pushed
It has energy only if it is hot
It has energy only when it is lit

quiz.p: By itself, heat energy moves from where to where?
quiz.why: Heat moves by itself only from warmer to cooler. In the Clicking Coin Test, heat moved from the warm room into the cold bottle.
opts: From a warmer thing to a cooler thing
From a cooler thing to a warmer thing
From a heavy thing to a light thing
From a big thing to a small thing

quiz.p: The coin on a freezer bottle stopped clicking. What is the most likely reason?
quiz.why: When the bottle matches the room, no more heat moves in. With no moving heat, the air stops swelling and the coin stops clicking.
opts: The bottle had warmed to room temperature
The bottle ran out of air

quiz.p: A fan blows on an ice cube and it melts faster. What did the fan do?
quiz.why: A fan only moves air. Moving air brings the room's heat to the ice faster, so the ice melts sooner.
opts: Moved the room's warm air onto the ice faster

quiz.p: A wire has fallen on a wet road. What should you do?
quiz.why: A fallen wire may still carry electricity, and wet ground or a wet stick can carry it to you. Keep far away and tell a grown-up.
opts: Stay far away and tell a grown-up
Push it aside with a stick

quiz.p: Why must your hands be dry before you touch a switch?
quiz.why: Water with salts in it carries electricity, and your body does too. Dry skin is much safer.
opts: Wet skin lets electricity pass more easily
Wet hands make the switch rust
Dry hands switch things on faster

quiz.p: An engine turns heat into movement. What must it have besides a hot place?
quiz.why: Heat does work only as it passes from a hotter place to a colder place. With no colder place, nothing makes the engine move.
opts: A colder place to send some heat to

applications: Power stations burn coal or use falling water or wind to turn turbines. The turbines turn generators, and wires carry the electricity to homes, hospitals and trains.
A solar water heater on a roof changes sunlight to heat. It saves cooking gas or electricity that a geyser would use.
A fridge and an air conditioner use electricity to move heat out of a cool place. That is why the back of a fridge feels warm.
A matka cools water with no electricity. Water seeps through the clay and dries on the outside, and drying carries heat away.
Energy ratings on fans, fridges and air conditioners tell you how much electricity each one uses for the same job.
A power cut stops pumps, lifts and fans. Hospitals keep batteries and diesel generators ready for such hours.
A cattle shed on the ground floor of a mountain house warms the rooms above with the heat of the animals' bodies.

open_questions.q: What is the energy of empty space, which scientists call dark energy?
open_questions.why_open: Measurements of far-away exploding stars show the universe growing faster and faster. Nobody knows what is behind it.

open_questions.q: Why was the early universe arranged so that heat flows from hot to cold?
open_questions.why_open: The rule that heat flows from hot to cold depends on the early universe having been very orderly. Nobody knows why it was.

open_questions.q: Can we store the Sun's energy cheaply enough to light every home all night?
open_questions.why_open: Batteries are improving fast. Nobody yet knows which kind of storage will be cheap and clean enough for everyone.

open_questions.q: Will the universe one day reach one temperature, so that nothing can happen?
open_questions.why_open: Some physicists expect this, a very long time from now. Others think the picture may change as we learn more about dark energy.

open_questions.q: How much of the energy in a meal does each body really use?
open_questions.why_open: People differ in how well they digest food and in how much heat they give out. Measuring it exactly for one person is hard.
