maths.problem: A freezer bottle clicked 14, 8, 4 and 2 times in four half-minutes. How many clicks in all, and how many in the first minute?
maths.answer: 28 clicks in all. 22 clicks in the first minute.
maths.explain: Add all four: 14 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 28. The first minute is the first two half-minutes: 14 + 8 = 22.
maths.context: This is about the Clicking Coin Test. A coin clicks on a freezer bottle and you count the clicks in each half minute.

chart.title: Made-up example: clicks in each half minute

maths.why_maths: Adding the counts gives the total clicks. Comparing the bars shows how fast the heat moved at each stage.

maths.problem: The clicks fell from 14 to 8 to 4 to 2. By what fraction did they fall each time? What does that say about the heat moving in?
maths.answer: They fell by about a half each time. The heat moved in more slowly as the bottle got closer to room temperature.
maths.explain: 8 is a little more than half of 14. 4 is half of 8. 2 is half of 4. The gap between the bottle and the room shrinks, so less heat moves in each half minute.
maths.context: This is about the Clicking Coin Test. The counts of clicks fall as the freezer bottle warms.
maths.why_maths: Finding the fraction shows a pattern: the smaller the gap, the slower the heat moves.

maths.problem: In the Fan and the Ice, a cube in the wind melted in 16 minutes and a cube behind the screen in 20 minutes. What fraction of the time did the wind take?
maths.answer: Four fifths of the time. The wind saved 4 minutes, one fifth.
maths.explain: 16 ÷ 20 = 4 ÷ 5, so the wind cube took four fifths of the time. 20 − 16 = 4 minutes saved, which is 4 out of 20, or one fifth.
maths.context: This is about the Fan and the Ice. Two cubes melt, one in the wind and one behind a screen.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of the time says how much faster one thing is, whatever the room's temperature.

maths.problem: A town uses 1,000 units of electricity in an hour, and 7 of every 10 units come from coal. How many units come from coal?
maths.explain: Seven out of every 10 units means 7 tenths of 1,000. One tenth of 1,000 is 1,000 ÷ 10 = 100, and 7 tenths is 100 × 7 = 700 units.
maths.context: This is about how electricity is made. In India about 7 of every 10 units still come from burning coal.
maths.why_maths: Turning 'seven in ten' into a number of units shows how large the coal share is.

maths.problem: A coal power station takes in 300 units of energy from burning coal and sends out 100 units as electricity. What fraction becomes electricity, and where does the rest go?
maths.answer: One third. The other two thirds leave as heat in the air and water.
maths.explain: 100 ÷ 300 = 1 ÷ 3. The energy that does not become electricity is 300 − 100 = 200 units, which spreads out as heat.
maths.context: This is about energy changers. A power station is a very large one, and it gives out much of its energy as heat.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows what share of the energy does the job we want.

maths.problem: Burning a 10 kilogram table would give out about 160 million joules. One unit of electricity is 3.6 million joules. About how many units is that?
maths.explain: 160 ÷ 3.6 is about 44.4. So the wood of a table holds as much energy as about 44 units of electricity.
maths.context: This is about the chemical energy in a table. A table is made of wood, and wood burns.
maths.why_maths: Dividing by 3.6 million turns a huge number of joules into units you can compare with an electricity bill.

maths.problem: A resting grown-up gives out about 90 watts of heat. How many watt-hours is that in one night of 8 hours? How many 9 watt LED bulbs is that?
maths.answer: 720 watt-hours. That is the same as ten 9 watt LED bulbs.
maths.explain: 90 watts for 8 hours is 90 × 8 = 720 watt-hours. Each 9 watt bulb gives out 9 watts. 90 ÷ 9 = 10, so a resting grown-up gives out as much heat as 10 such bulbs.
maths.context: This is about living bodies as energy changers. A sleeping body gives out heat all night.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying watts by hours gives energy, and comparing with bulbs makes the number easy to picture.

roots.context: We have found that a still table holds energy, and that energy makes something happen only when it moves. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Clicking Coin Test, a room-warm bottle did nothing on the table. A freezer bottle made the coin click until the bottle was as warm as the room. The room-warm bottle held plenty of heat energy, and it gave away as much as it took in. So while the same amount of heat passes in each direction, nothing shows. A click comes only when more heat passes in one direction than in the other.
deep_truth.habit: We say that a thing which does nothing has no energy, as if energy belonged only to things that move. 'Still' only describes how a thing looks from the outside. Inside, the particles are always moving.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Clicking Coin Test, the room-warm bottle held heat energy and its coin stayed still. In the Fan and the Ice, moving air carried the room's heat to the ice, and the ice melted sooner. In both, things happened only where one thing was warmer than another.

three.who_am_i: You are warm because your body turns food into heat every second. You hold heat energy like the table does, and you pass it on to every cooler thing you touch.
three.what_is_life: A living being stays warmer than the room by using the energy of food. She keeps eating, so she keeps giving her warmth out into the world around her.
three.what_is_this_world: Everything holds energy. What happens in the world happens where there is a difference, such as warm next to cool or high next to low.

roots.thread: A table, a bottle, the air and your hand all hold heat energy of the same kind. When they are all at one temperature, they trade energy equally in both directions, so nothing shows. When something cold is put beside them, the trade is no longer equal, and then a coin clicks or ice melts. So the quiet and the click come from the same energy. A still room looks calm, but heat is passing between things in every direction all the time.

teachings.link: A still table is quiet on the outside. Inside, its particles never stop shaking. Stillness is a balance of many small movements, and movement begins when the balance is broken.

science.text: Albert Einstein showed in 1905 that mass is a store of energy. A 10 kilogram table holds about 900 million billion joules of energy in its mass, though nobody can take it out.

other_view.view: Energy is a number that stays the same through every change. The shaking of particles and the passing of heat between things follow the laws of motion. These laws already explain everything we see, so most physicists say that nothing more needs to be added.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out when heat can do work? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1824 a young French engineer named Sadi Carnot asked why English steam engines did more work than French ones from the same coal. Many engineers believed that a better engine would one day turn all the heat of its fire into movement. Carnot thought about water mills. A mill works only when water falls from a higher place to a lower one. The work depends on the height of the fall. He wrote that heat is the same. It makes things move only as it passes from a hot place to a colder place. So even a perfect engine must let some heat go into the cooler air. He published this in a small book, Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire. Few people read it. Carnot died of cholera in 1832, aged 36. Later, William Thomson and Rudolf Clausius studied his book and built the science of heat from it.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a good enough engine could turn all the heat from its fuel into movement. Carnot showed that heat does work only as it falls from hot to cold, so some heat must always pass to a colder place.

playtest: The experiments and activities in this lesson were reasoned through step by step. They have not yet been tried at home. Please treat the amounts as a starting point. The Clicking Coin Test (core) needs three glass bottles with narrow mouths and a coin wider than the mouth. A plastic bottle usually does not click, because its soft sides give way. Cool the bottles for at least 30 minutes. If a freezer bottle gives no clicks, check three things. The coin must cover the whole mouth, the coin must be wet, and nobody should have warmed the bottle with their hands. The number of clicks depends on the bottle and the room. Expect the order from most to fewest to be freezer, then fridge, then room. Never pour hot water on a cold bottle. The Fan and the Ice (core) needs a wind screen that really stops the wind from reaching one plate. Hang a tissue strip behind it to check. If the two cubes melt at the same speed, move the plates or use a wider screen. A light fan may show only a small gap. Light Out for Half an Hour needs a grown-up at the main switch. Do not do it if anyone at home needs a machine that runs on electricity. The Sail Race keeps water away from the fan: put the fan on a dry stool and dry your hands before touching it. The street survey needs a grown-up beside the child at every door. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026: Kavaratti plant (2005), Bengaluru street lights (1905), Carnot dates, the Einstein and Feynman citations and about 7 in 10 units from coal (the figure changes each year).
